The decode instance then allocates destination blocks, prepares the NIXL transfer, and initiates NIXL READ to pull the KV blocks from the prefill instance. Because these coordination and setup steps occur sequentially after prefill and before decoding can begin, they extend the TTFT critical path, as shown in the following timeline.

Figure 1: Pull-mode KV transfer timeline, where the router relay, decode-side allocation, and NIXL READ run serially on the path to the first token

This post introduces a push-based NIXL connector that moves post-prefill transfer coordination and setup off the critical path. If you run disaggregated prefill/decode inference with vLLM, push mode can improve application responsiveness by reducing TTFT and TPOT, particularly at high request rates.

In our benchmark on a 1P1D deployment using Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) P5en instances connected with EFA, push mode delivered up to 3x better TTFT and up to 30 percent better time-per-output-token (TPOT) compared to pull mode (see the Performance data section) for the Qwen3-32B model. Results depend on workload and configuration.

We built and validated the feature on AWS Trainium instance clusters connected with EFA, and then we contributed it to vLLM as an accelerator-agnostic feature. The results here are from an Amazon EC2 P5en (GPU) cluster with EFA, showing the gains carry over to GPUs. This post explains the push-based architecture, transfer flow, threading model, performance results, and how to reproduce the benchmark.

Push-based KV transfer

This section explains the push-based design: its architecture, the transfer protocol, and the threading model that keeps KV transfer off the critical path.

Architecture overview

Push-based transfer improves TTFT and decode throughput for two reasons:

  • It removes the serialization of the pull model by overlapping producer and consumer work. The decode instance registers its target blocks in advance while the producer is still computing KV. The transfer then begins as soon as the producer’s blocks are ready, rather than after a consumer-side ID-discovery round trip, removing that round trip from the path to first token.
  • It moves the transfer-setup time off the decode instance. That setup runs on the prefill side and on a background thread. It prepares the NIXL descriptors and submits the transfer, so the decode instance does not spend those cycles during its latency-critical token-generation phase.

The net effect is lower TTFT and higher output-token throughput on the decode instance.

The push connector coordinates three actors: the decode instance registers its target blocks up front, the prefill instance matches each request and issues the transfer, and a dedicated background thread carries the KV write off the engine’s forward-pass loop. The following diagram shows how these pieces fit together.

Figure 2: Push-based KV transfer architecture, showing how the decode instance, prefill instance, and background transfer thread coordinate

Implementation details

The protocol has three logical steps.

1. Registration (decode side). When the decode instance allocates local blocks for a request requiring remote prefilling, it prepares a registration describing where the prefill instance should write the KV: its own identity and the block locations it has just reserved. Within the same engine step, the worker transmits this registration to the prefill instance as a NIXL notification. Because registration happens at allocation time, the connector knows the destination blocks before the prefill instance completes prefill.

2. Rendezvous (prefill side). The registration from the decoder and the completion of prefill on the producer can arrive in either order, and the connector handles both. If the registration arrives first, the producer holds it until its own prefill finishes. If prefill finishes first, the producer holds the request’s blocks until the registration arrives. Whichever event happens second triggers the transfer. The connector pairs requests by ID, and the matching accounts for reissued requests, correctly associating preempted or retried requests.

3. Transfer (prefill side). Once a request is matched, the producer establishes a connection to the decode instance (if one does not already exist) and issues an NIXL WRITE that copies the KV blocks directly into the decoder’s registered memory, addressing each destination tensor-parallel rank. The producer and consumer may use different internal block layouts. Each side maps block locations to its own physical layout at transfer time, allowing different block sizes on each side. Each WRITE carries a completion notification that NIXL delivers to the decode instance once the data arrives. The decoder counts these notifications, one per producer rank that writes into it. It treats the KV as received only after all expected notifications have arrived, at which point the request proceeds to decode.

Threading model

The push connector separates model execution from KV-transfer preparation by using a dedicated background transfer thread on each prefill worker. At the start of a request, the decode main loop allocates its destination KV blocks and registers them with the prefill instance while the prefill main loop computes the prompt KV cache. After both the destination registration and prompt KV are ready, the prefill main loop hands the KV blocks to the background thread and quickly returns to model execution.

The background thread establishes or reuses the NIXL connection, maps the request’s KV block IDs to memory descriptors, merges contiguous blocks into larger transfer regions, and submits the NIXL WRITE to the decode instance. When NIXL completes the transfer, it sends a completion notification to the decode instance, which then begins token generation. Keeping descriptor preparation and transfer submission off the latency-critical main loops prevents this per-request work from delaying model execution. The following diagram shows these main-loop and background-thread handoffs for a single request.

Figure 3: Main-loop and background-thread handoffs for a single request in the push-based threading model

Timing comparison of pull and push

The following diagram summarizes the pull and push transfer flows described in the preceding sections and highlights their effect on TTFT. Although both modes use the same NIXL and EFA/RDMA data path, pull performs the metadata relay and decode-side setup after prefill, while push overlaps decode-side setup with prefill. As a result, push removes these operations from the post-prefill critical path, allowing decoding to begin sooner.

Figure 4: Pull and push transfer flows compared, highlighting how push overlaps decode-side setup with prefill

The two modes also involve a routing tradeoff. Pull mode allows the router to select a decode instance after prefill completes, which provides greater flexibility for load-aware routing and quality-of-service management. Push mode selects the decode instance earlier so that destination setup can overlap with prefill. In return, under comparable load, the prefill instance can release its KV blocks sooner because the transfer starts as soon as both the prompt KV and destination registration are ready.

Performance data

For evaluation, we used Qwen3-32B model on a 1P1D deployment using Amazon EC2 P5en instances connected with EFA. To isolate P→D transfer performance, we configured the benchmark to disable prefix caching with --no-enable-prefix-caching. This configuration makes the decode node retrieve the full KV cache from the prefill node for every request. Otherwise, overlapping prompts could reuse the decode node’s local cache and bypass the transfer, which would produce misleading comparison results.

The following chart compares TTFT for push and pull KV transfer. We sweep input lengths 1k–16k and request rates of 1–8 queries per second (QPS). At low load and short prompts, the two modes perform almost identically. As QPS and input length grow, pull mode degrades sharply, reaching about 1,744 ms at 8 QPS and 16k. Push mode stays far lower at roughly 540 ms, around 3x reduction. The gap opens because pull mode posts NIXL descriptors inline on the decode worker, synchronously within its engine loop, so that work stalls token generation. Push mode moves it to a background thread, off the critical path.

Figure 5: TTFT for push compared to pull KV transfer across input lengths and request rates (1P1D topology, 128 output tokens, prefix caching disabled on the decode node)

This chart shows TPOT under the same conditions. The pattern mirrors TTFT. At light load, push and pull are close, around 5.6–5.8 ms. As load and input length rise, pull climbs to about 10.4 ms at 4–8 QPS and 16k, while push holds near 7 ms. The reason is that push offloads descriptor preparation and transfer submission from the decode worker. Token generation is not starved, so per-token latency stays flat even at high concurrency and long contexts.

Figure 6: TPOT for push compared to pull KV transfer across input lengths and request rates (1P1D topology, 128 output tokens, prefix caching disabled on the decode node)

How to run benchmark

To reproduce our 1P1D benchmark configuration, one prefill node and one decode node, using Amazon EC2 P5en instances connected with EFA, refer to the detailed instructions in the Reproducing our results guide. The guide covers environment setup, launching the vLLM prefill and decode servers, running the benchmark, and collecting results. The feature can run on other supported configurations, but performance results will vary depending on the hardware, model, workload, and network configuration.

Conclusion

In this post, we showed how the push-based KV connector overlaps prefill computation with decode-side block allocation and registration, removing the post-prefill router round trip and decode-side transfer setup from the critical path. This reduces TTFT and TPOT, particularly at high request rates. In our Qwen3-32B benchmark on a 1P1D deployment using Amazon EC2 P5en instances connected with EFA, push mode provided up to a 3x improvement in TTFT and 30 percent improvement in TPOT compared with pull mode. Results vary by workload and configuration. To use push mode, configure both the prefill and decode servers to use NixlPushConnector instead of NixlConnector.

Choose the push-based connector when early decode node selection is acceptable and lower TTFT is the priority. The pull-based connector remains the better fit for workloads that require bidirectional KV transfer or defer decode-instance selection until after prefill for load-aware routing. vLLM supports both push- and pull-based KV connectors, so you can select the approach that best fits your deployment.

As a future improvement, we are exploring bringing the background NIXL threading model to the pull-mode connector, moving NIXL setup off the critical path so that pull-mode workloads could benefit from the same optimizations. We have opened a pull request to explore this.

Related resources

  • vLLM disaggregated serving guide
  • AWS EFA
  • Push-mode NIXL KV connector

Acknowledgments

We thank the vLLM community for their support in maintaining this feature.

About the authors

item.title: [Amazon Bedrock] Improve TTFT for multi-turn agentic workloads with bi-direct…
item.description: Full title: Improve TTFT for multi-turn agentic workloads with bi-directional KV transfer in vLLM
item.content:encoded:
Artificial Intelligence

Improve TTFT for multi-turn agentic workloads with bi-directional KV transfer in vLLM

Multi-turn agentic workloads build on accumulated context as an agent reasons, invokes tools, and incorporates earlier results. With each new turn, the client resends the conversation history, including system instructions, prior prompts, tool results, and model responses, causing the growing context to be processed repeatedly. In Prefill-decode (P-D) disaggregation, each request is split across specialized nodes: the prefill node processes the prompt and builds its key-value (KV) cache, then the decode node retrieves those KV blocks and generates the response.

Conventional disaggregated serving, however, only transfers KV cache in one direction: from prefill to decode node. This one-directional flow creates two inefficiencies for multi-turn workloads. First, after generating a response, the decode node holds KV cache entries for both the prompt and the newly generated tokens. When processing the next turn, the prefill node cannot retrieve those entries, so it must recompute the KV projections for the previous response tokens. Second, the decode node maintains the session state while the prefill nodes don’t, increasing the probability of cache eviction for active sessions on the prefill nodes. On a full cache miss, the prefill node must recompute KV projections for the entire conversation history, including system instructions, prior user requests, tool results, and model-generated responses. As the conversation grows, this redundant work consumes more accelerator capacity and increases time to first token (TTFT).

When you build conversational assistants and agentic applications, longer interaction histories can increase latency and consume accelerator capacity through repeated prefill computation. In this post, we show how bi-directional KV cache transfer lets prefill and decode nodes reuse previously computed context across turns, which improves accelerator utilization and helps applications sustain responsive TTFT as conversations grow.

In our multi-turn benchmarks on a 1P1D deployment using Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) P5en instances, bi-directional KV transfer reduced TTFT by up to 1.6x for Qwen3-32B and up to 3.3x for zai-org/GLM-5-FP8 (see the Performance data section). Results vary with workload and configuration. The instances are connected with AWS Elastic Fabric Adapter (AWS EFA), a low-latency remote direct memory access (RDMA) network used across servers in AWS. On supported instance types, AWS EFA supports GPUDirect RDMA and Neuron Direct RDMA to move KV blocks directly between GPU or AWS Trainium device memory on the prefill and decode nodes.

We originally built and validated the feature on AWS Trainium instance clusters connected with EFA and contributed it to vLLM as an accelerator-agnostic capability. The results presented here are from an Amazon EC2 P5en GPU cluster with EFA, showing that the benefits also carry over to GPUs. This post explains the bi-directional KV transfer architecture, router metadata flow, KV-block retention and recompute controls, performance results, and how to reproduce the benchmark.

Bi-directional KV transfer

Bi-directional KV transfer is a mechanism in which a decode node returns previously computed KV to a prefill node on subsequent turns of a conversation. This avoids recomputing shared context on the prefill node and is governed by a configurable KV recompute threshold. It mitigates both computational-redundancy scenarios described earlier. To make it work, the KV must survive past the turn that produced it and travel in the reverse direction, coordinated by a KV-cache-aware router.

NIXL KV connector enhancements for bi-directional transfer

We extended the NVIDIA Inference Xfer Library (NIXL) KV connector to let prefill nodes consume remote KV blocks, similar to how decode nodes already consume KV blocks that the prefill node provides. This is not a trivial change, because the two node types are architecturally different: prefill nodes compute KV representations for new prompt tokens and can provide complete prompt KV blocks. Decode nodes lack the capability (or efficiency) to generate complete KV representations and can only serve previously cached KV blocks. As a result, prefill and decode nodes still carry their own roles and logic for computing the metadata of remote and local KV blocks. The actual KV transfer mechanism (a NIXL READ), however, is common to both the P->D and D->P directions.

The following diagram first shows the existing flow in blue. The router sends the request to prefill node, prefill node computes the prompt KV and returns its block metadata, and the router forwards the request and metadata to decode node for the standard P→D NIXL READ. The numbered red path illustrates the bi-directional KV transfer additions: (1) decode node retains eligible KV blocks after generation, (2) returns their metadata in the streaming response, and (3) the router caches that metadata for the next prefill request. Prefill node then (4) checks the remotely reusable KV after it applies local cache matches, (5) queues an asynchronous receive when the reusable token count meets the threshold, and (6) performs a D→P NIXL READ before computing the remaining suffix.

Figure 1: Standard prefill-to-decode flow (blue) and the bi-directional KV transfer additions (red)

KV-cache-aware router

vLLM includes connector-side support for bi-directional KV transfer, while coordinating KV reuse across conversation turns requires a KV-cache-aware router. vLLM GitHub provides an example proxy that implements the flow used in this post which can be adapted for your environment.

The KV-cache-aware router is a lightweight, stateful control-plane component between the client, prefill, and decode nodes. It maintains an in-memory mapping from the client-provided conversation_id to decode’s kv_transfer_params. The router stores only block-location metadata, not KV tensors, and obtains that metadata from the response stream rather than separately querying decode node.

The following diagram shows how the router manages KV metadata across conversation turns. On the first turn, the cache lookup misses and the request follows the standard P→D flow. The router then saves decode’s metadata from the response stream. On later turns, the router retrieves that metadata using the conversation_id so prefill can reuse KV from decode. It then refreshes the metadata after generation for the next turn.

Figure 2: KV-cache-aware router metadata flow across conversation turns

Block retention TTL

Normally a decode instance frees a request’s blocks as soon as generation finishes. Under bi-directional KV transfer mode, it holds them for a configurable lifetime (decoder_kv_blocks_ttl, default 480 seconds) and publishes their location and expiry. The conversation’s KV, both prompt prefix and generated response, then stays available for the next turn. For a turn that arrives before the time to live (TTL) expires, prefill node reuses the KV. One that arrives later falls back to normal prefill. Because this TTL is fixed and not renewed, tune it to the expected time between turns to balance KV reuse against accelerator-memory usage. A natural next improvement is to extend the heartbeat-renewed lease to the decode side. A decode instance could then reclaim blocks as soon as a conversation goes idle rather than at the end of a fixed timer.

KV recompute threshold

KV reuse isn’t always faster than local recomputation. For a short reusable prefix, interconnect and coordination overhead can exceed the time needed to recompute the tokens. The kv_recompute_threshold setting, which defaults to 64 tokens, controls this decision. Prefill node recomputes when the token count to compute is below the threshold and pulls KV from decode node when it is at or above the threshold. Deployments can tune this value based on model computation time, KV size, and interconnect performance.

Performance data

For evaluation, we used Qwen3-32B and GLM-5-FP8 models on a 1P1D deployment using Amazon EC2 P5en instances connected with EFA. To emulate scenarios in which the prefill node has evicted its local cache or the router selects a different prefill node that does not have the conversation’s KV blocks, we disabled prefix caching on prefill node with --no-enable-prefix-caching.

Across both the models, turning on bi-directional KV transfer reduces prefill computation on multi-turn conversations, and the benefit typically grows with prompt length. With the feature OFF, the prefill instance recomputes the entire grown context each turn, so TTFT rises steeply. Qwen3-32B climbs from 158 ms at 2k to 778 ms at 24k, and GLM-5-FP8 from 500 ms at 2k to 2,334 ms at 20k. With it ON, the decode instance’s retained KV is reused instead of recomputed, keeping TTFT far flatter. Qwen3-32B rises only from 122 ms to 460 ms over the same range (about a 1.6x reduction at the longest prompt), while GLM-5-FP8 rises from 358 ms to 702 ms and runs up to 3.3x below the recompute path at long prompts. The prefill-duration breakdown explains why.

Bi-directional transfer adds a small KV-transfer time (about 30 ms to 130 ms for Qwen3-32B; about 29 ms to 110 ms for GLM-5-FP8), but the prefill compute it removes far outweighs that KV-transfer time. As a result, the total prefill duration with transfer ON (Qwen3-32B: 128 ms to 414 ms; GLM-5-FP8: 316 ms to 541 ms) stays well below the recompute-only path (Qwen3-32B: 153 ms to 744 ms; GLM-5-FP8: 500 ms to 2,331 ms). The larger GLM-5-FP8 model shows a bigger absolute and relative gap, since its higher per-token recompute time makes KV reuse pay off even more as models and contexts scale.

Qwen3-32B

The following chart plots TTFT against prompt length for Qwen3-32B, comparing bi-directional KV transfer ON versus OFF.

Figure 3: Qwen3-32B TTFT versus prompt length with bi-directional KV transfer on and off

The next chart breaks the prefill duration for the same runs into its recompute and KV-transfer components.

Figure 4: Qwen3-32B prefill duration split into recompute and KV-transfer components

Together the charts show TTFT staying nearly flat with the feature ON while the OFF path climbs steeply as context grows, because the small KV-transfer time is far outweighed by the recompute it removes.

zai-org/GLM-5-FP8

The same two views follow for GLM-5-FP8. The first plots TTFT against prompt length with the feature ON versus OFF.

Figure 5: zai-org/GLM-5-FP8 TTFT with KV reuse on and off

The second breaks the prefill duration into its recompute and KV-transfer components.

Figure 6: zai-org/GLM-5-FP8 prefill duration breakdown

GLM-5-FP8 shows a much larger gap than Qwen3-32B, up to about 3.3x lower TTFT at long prompts, because its higher per-token recompute time makes KV reuse pay off even more as context length grows.

How to run benchmark

To reproduce our 1P1D benchmark configuration, one prefill node and one decode node, using Amazon EC2 P5en instances with EFA, follow the step-by-step instructions in the Reproducing our results guide. The guide covers environment setup, launching the vLLM prefill and decode servers, running the benchmark, and collecting results. The feature can run on other supported configurations, but performance results will vary depending on the hardware, model, workload, and network configuration.

Conclusion

In this post, we showed how bi-directional KV cache transfer can reduce TTFT as an agent’s conversation history grows. In P-D disaggregated deployments, the feature lets prefill node reuse KV blocks retained by decode node across turns, reducing repeated computation. Configurable block-retention and recompute thresholds determine when reuse occurs. On a 1P1D deployment using Amazon EC2 P5en instances connected with EFA, at the longest prompt lengths tested, we observed TTFT reductions of 1.6x for Qwen3-32B and 3.3x for zai-org/GLM-5-FP8. Results depend on the workload and deployment configuration. To implement this in your environment, use vLLM v0.21.0 or later with NixlConnector, enable bidirectional_kv_xfer on both prefill and decode servers, use a kv-cache-aware router, and follow the GitHub reproduction guide.

Related resources

  • AWS EFA
  • Prefill-Decode (P-D) disaggregated serving
  • Benchmark KV Cache Offloading with Multi-Turn Conversations

Acknowledgments

We thank the vLLM community for their support in maintaining this feature.

About the author

item.description: Full title: Together Post-Training: frontier-grade model shaping, the way that fits you
item.content:encoded:
All blog posts

Fine-Tuning

Published 10/19/2026

Together Post-Training: frontier-grade model shaping, the way that fits you

  • AuthorsIvan Provilkov, Gleb Khaykin, Denis Mazur, Nikita Smetanin, Egor Timofeev, Conner Manuel, Felix Zhang, Alex Mazitov, Jasmine Li, Gleb Vazhenin, Sergei Vorobyov, Qingyang Wu, Derek Petersen, Arseniy Belorukov, Artem Chumachenko, Aman Singhal, Alpay Ariyak, Jisen Li, Vladimir Malinovskii, Maksim Abraham, Zhongzhu Zhou, Denis Fedorenko, Sonny Khan, David Wang, Jennifer Wu, Max Ryabinin
  • Table of contents40+ Models Chosen for Production...40+ Models Chosen for Production...40+ Models Chosen for Production...

We are introducing Together Post-Training, a new service for building custom models on our platform — both from environment rewards via RL and supervision data via SFT. This service is designed to give you flexible and efficient model shaping without the heavy infra burden.

Together Post-Training makes it easy to define the training loop, while we co-optimize the systems and infrastructure underneath for model quality and training speed. Nothing now stands between you and the best model that is uniquely yours.

The value of custom models

In 2026, training custom models for your AI workloads is no longer a niche topic. Companies are actively exploring it to reduce costs and improve task-specific performance. Instead of fixing model behaviors and improving their efficiency via context or harness engineering, many AI-native and AI-forward organizations are training specialist agents, matching the quality of frontier models at a fraction of the cost and runtime. On top of that, training the model yourself yields greater ownership and flexibility: the resulting checkpoint can be deployed in any location, further refined, or even used locally.

At Together, we want to empower every AI developer with the ability to get the best model for their task, as conveniently as possible. Post-training a great model requires many iterations on data curation, training algorithms, and evaluation protocols. On top of that, infrastructure for RL is getting ever more complex, with a fine line between “an efficiency optimization” and “a silent bug that holds back your runs”. Doing so for large models reliably and at scale presents its own set of challenges.

Frontier labs have entire teams solving each of the above problems. Since tackling all challenges at once is a big investment, many companies that could benefit from post-training never start it, or start and stall. Together Post-Training handles all optimizations and infrastructure without getting in the way, and our forward-deployed team partners with our customers to help with the end-to-end workflow. This lets every researcher or domain expert focus on what they do best while we take care of the rest.

Together Post-Training at a glance

As the complexity of post-training continues to evolve, so should the tooling around it. Together Post-Training provides a set of common abstractions familiar to ML developers, as well as control over the resources used by each experiment, while making sure that all computations under the hood are fast, cost-efficient, and, most importantly, correct.

We built our service to offer the highest degree of flexibility for your experiments. You can run LoRA training, including multiple LoRA adapters sharing the same GPU capacity, as well as full-weight experiments for select models. In contrast to our fine-tuning service, the entire training loop of Together Post-Training is yours to define. You can use any data, environments, or agentic harnesses that suit your setup best, and add any steps you need (such as logging or external benchmarking) throughout the training process. The entire workflow is as follows:

A high-level summary of using Together Post-Training. Left: commands executed on the user side, right: service components running on Together’s side.

All experiments run on Model Resources — GPU allocations that are fully yours, not competing with others’ requests for priority. Each Model Resource can hold one or several Training Sessions, where each one corresponds to a single experiment using the same base model (for example, one set of LoRA adapters). This means you get the best rollout and training performance, as you never have to compete with other users’ requests executing on the same hardware. At the same time, dedicated GPU allocations mean you can run full-weight finetuning, going beyond LoRA when adapting to large knowledge-intensive tasks.

Once you allocate the model resource and start the session, you can execute each step of the training loop. Each session contains a Trainer instance responsible for running forward/backward steps and updating the weights, as well as Generator instances for executing rollouts from the policy. For every model, we heavily optimize training and rollout performance, making sure all operations are fast and numerically aligned across stacks. In the case of SFT, you can start a model resource with 0 generators to save costs. You decide the point at which the trainer parameters are sent to the generator; we also support asynchronous RL for high GPU utilization of both components at all times, especially with long agentic rollouts.

While we support a number of standard losses (from cross-entropy and GRPO to CISPO and DPPO), we also allow computing a custom training objective locally and sending its gradients to the Trainer for computing the updates.

Example of training with a custom loss from Together Post-Training docs

Together Post-Training launches with a range of leading open-weight models, including Muse Spark Open, GLM 5.3, Kimi K3, and Qwen 3.8-27B. We will expand the selection in the coming weeks, making sure you can use both the highest-capability frontier LLMs and efficient smaller models.

Quality, performance, and efficiency

Delegating the internals of post-training infrastructure can be a daunting decision. Our team has first-hand experience catching silent bugs in complex machine learning systems, from pushing the frontier of RL research to training LLMs that have served millions of users. We understand that the best training stack is the one that gets you the best model, and building such infrastructure demands careful implementation and co-design across all components.

For these reasons, we prioritized quality of output models as our north star in the development of the service. One notorious example of issues affecting RL results is the alignment between training and inference engines: if the same model weights produce slightly different outputs due to mismatching numerics, the whole run might underperform or even collapse. We eliminate numerous sources of policy drift across training and inference, using both standard techniques like Rollout Routing Replay and advanced optimizations driven by our research in training stability.

Beyond model quality, we also work to make each run as fast and as efficient as possible, because post-training requires multiple iterations: the sooner a run finishes and the less it costs, the more ideas you get to test. Most of the time in RL is spent on generating rollouts, which allows us to capitalize on years of research and engineering behind Together’s inference products. Our rollout engines draw on the same optimizations as our serving stack. For multi-turn agents, intelligent caching and routing minimize redundant computations while keeping memory costs bounded. On the training side, optimized parallelism and sequence packing speed up both SFT and RL steps.

With Together Post-Training, you size each experiment to what it needs and do not pay more. If your experiment is bottlenecked by rollout concurrency, you can request the exact number of sampler replicas. Several LoRA experiments can share one model resource, so running a sweep doesn’t mean reserving more GPUs for every setup. We bill every model resource per GPU-minute, yet thanks to many optimizations of our dedicated and multi-LoRA serving stacks, the overall costs of training drop below token-based pricing as soon as you scale up the experiments.

Optimized deployment after training

When the post-training experiments are finished, it might be important to run each resulting model side by side to compare their outputs. We now support multi-LoRA adapter serving in Dedicated Model Inference: instead of starting a separate production deployment for each run, you can swap the adapters at your convenience in a single GPU deployment, helping you lower the serving costs.

Lastly, converting the model to run at the highest throughput in production means it potentially executes in lower precision, in a different hardware configuration, and with different kernels compared to rollout generation. Through a combination of algorithmic and systems improvements, we ensure that each training checkpoint retains the quality in serving, even after switching from multi-LoRA sampling to a fully performant merged inference in FP4 precision.

Getting started

To begin your first post-training experiments, install the latest Together SDK and read the docs. We also provide a selection of cookbooks that can help you get started with Together Post-Training, which are available at github.com/togethercomputer/post-training-cookbook. These cookbooks provide examples of training with GRPO on a standard GSM8K benchmark, implementing DPO as a custom loss, or training multiple LoRA adapters within the same model resource. If you already have a setup that uses post-training services such as Tinker API, we also offer a simple way to migrate from them. You can replace one line in your scripts, and everything else can stay the same:

-import tinker
+import together.post_training.tinker as tinker

Read our Tinker migration guide to learn more.

How AI-native companies are using Together Post-Training today

Before this launch, we worked with a select group of organizations pushing the frontier of custom models. We granted them early access to our service over the past few months; the feedback we received was invaluable in developing the product which now everyone can use. Hear from the teams themselves:

“We had a great experience with the Together Post-Training platform from day one. The high degree of control and flexibility let us start running real RL experiments within a couple of hours. The service is efficient, allowing us to run up to five concurrent RL experiments on the same GPU capacity. The Together Research team was an exceptional collaborator throughout the training process, giving us feedback on model selection, training techniques, reward functions, and training efficiency.”

– Anthony Li, Associate Director of Data Science, Deel

“At Jack & Jill, we build two AI agents: Jack for professionals, and Jill for companies, who recruit from Jack’s network of professionals who’ve opted in to being introduced. We used Together Post-Training to post-train a model that predicts which candidates a hiring manager will want to meet, a core step in Jill’s search. Onboarding was easy, their team helped design our experiments, and their forward-deployed engineers wrote the scripts that got us to first results. We matched a closed-source model’s quality in offline evaluations, using an open-source model that’s significantly cheaper to serve.”

– Oliver Normand, Founding Engineer, Jack & Jill

“We’ve been collaborating with the Together team since the launch of its Post-Training beta in April. With the latest iteration, seamless self-onboarding made it easy to quickly launch full-scale agentic RL runs. The Post-Training service has proven to be exceptionally intuitive, flexible, and powerful for scaling sophisticated agentic workloads.”

– Adit Jain, Researcher, Collinear AI

Build with Together Post-Training

With the launch of Together Post-Training, we’re turning frontier-grade model customization into a reliable, flexible and efficient service. The next step is for you to make the most of it. For the first eight weeks, we are offering Together Post-Training at a reduced price of $9 per GPU-hour of B200 usage. Learn how to get started today — we’re excited to see what you will build.

But you don’t have to do this alone. For companies that want a partner, our forward-deployed engineers work alongside your team across the full post-training lifecycle. They’ll start with helping select the right open model and agent harness for your use case, work with you on your data and training environments, and then help with evaluations and shipping your own optimized endpoint.

If you would like to collaborate with Together on training models for your organization, feel free to reach out to us.

item.title: [DeepInfra] Granite 4.2 8B API Review: Providers Compared
item.content:encoded:
Granite 4.2 8B API Review: Providers Compared

Published on 2026.10.19 by DeepInfra

Granite 4.2 8B API Review Summary

AttributeDetails
Creator / TypeIBM, open-weights model
Release DateAugust 25, 2026
ReasoningYes, a reasoning model with built-in chain-of-thought
ModalitiesText in, text out (not multimodal, no image input)
Context Window131,072 tokens (about 197 A4 pages), with a long-context extension to 512K
Size / License / Weights8B parameters, Apache 2.0, weights on Hugging Face (ibm-granite/granite-4.2-8b)
Intelligence11 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, ranked 35th of 141 models and above the median of 8 for similar-size open-weight models
Cost$0.06 per 1M input tokens, $0.25 per 1M output tokens, a 75% cache discount, and about $0.02 per Intelligence Index task
Speed98.4 output tokens per second, above the median of about 75
Latency (TTFT)0.85 seconds, better than the 1.17-second median
Verbosity130M output tokens generated across the Intelligence Index, against a median of 82M
AvailabilityAvailable through two API providers, CoreWeave and DeepInfra, with pricing that varies by provider

Introduction to Granite 4.2 8B

Granite 4.2 8B is the mid-size reasoning model in IBM’s Granite 4.2 family. IBM positions it as a balanced model for general-purpose enterprise applications. Built-in chain-of-thought reasoning inside <think>…</think> tags supports strong results on reasoning-heavy benchmarks such as AIME 2025 (86.67) and LiveCodeBench v6 (73.24).

Three thinking modes let you balance depth against latency on each query: full thinking (the default), non-thinking, and low-effort.

The model is a decoder-only dense transformer. It uses grouped query attention (32 attention heads and 8 KV heads), rotary position embeddings (RoPE), and an MLP with SwiGLU activation.

It supports 12 languages: English, German, Spanish, French, Japanese, Portuguese, Arabic, Czech, Italian, Korean, Dutch, and Chinese.

Key capabilities

  • Built-in reasoning: Native chain-of-thought improves performance on math, coding, and complex multi-step problems.
  • Flexible thinking modes: You can switch between full thinking, non-thinking, and low-effort modes within a single model.
  • Reasoning-augmented tool calling: The model reasons about which tool to call, and why, before it makes the call.
  • Agentic workflows: Reinforcement learning covered software engineering on real repositories, multi-step terminal tasks, and multi-hop web search.

API Providers Comparison

Artificial Analysis tracks two providers for Granite 4.2 8B: DeepInfra and CoreWeave. OpenRouter routes between them, and Puter.js offers a free developer integration.

ProviderBlended Price (per 1M tokens)Output SpeedLatency (median first chunk)Key Differentiator
DeepInfra$0.05120 t/s0.77 sLowest input and cache prices ($0.06 and $0.015 per 1M) and the highest measured output speed
CoreWeave$0.0789 t/s0.74 sLowest output price ($0.15 per 1M) and slightly lower first-chunk latency
OpenRouter$0.06 in / $0.25 out on the DeepInfra routeDepends on the routed providerDepends on the routed providerAutomatic failover between DeepInfra and CoreWeave through one OpenAI-compatible API
Puter.jsFree to developers under a user-pays modelNot publishedNot publishedFree integration with no backend or API key setup

Latency in the table is the median time to the first chunk. A reasoning model also spends time thinking before its first answer token. Artificial Analysis measures that time at 17.78 seconds on DeepInfra and 22.65 seconds on CoreWeave.

OpenRouter’s own provider table shows the same ordering on throughput, with DeepInfra ahead of CoreWeave.

Best API Options

Three options cover most use cases:

API OptionWhy It’s a Strong Choice
DeepInfra (Recommended)DeepInfra offers the lowest input and cache prices, a $0.05 blended rate, and the highest measured output speed of the providers Artificial Analysis tracks. The Apache 2.0 weights make the model easy to host, which gives you a managed API without self-hosting overhead.
CoreWeaveCoreWeave suits workloads where output volume dominates the bill, thanks to its $0.15 per 1M output price. Its first-chunk latency is on par with DeepInfra.
OpenRouterOpenRouter provides automatic failover between the two providers through OpenAI-compatible endpoints, which simplifies integration. It reports 99.98% availability over 72 hours.

Limitations of the Model

Granite 4.2 8B has several limitations to weigh before you deploy it:

  • Verbosity: The model generated 130M output tokens across the Intelligence Index, against a median of 82M. Longer outputs raise output costs, so budget for them.
  • Reasoning latency: Time to the first answer token includes thinking time. Non-thinking and low-effort modes cut that wait for latency-sensitive requests.
  • Memory footprint: Weights take roughly 16 GB in bfloat16, and 4-bit quantized builds shrink that to roughly 4 to 6 GB. The KV cache grows with context length and concurrency, so serving the full 131K window needs far more memory than the weights alone.
  • Multilingual variance: Fine-tuning relied mostly on English instruction-response pairs, so multilingual dialog quality may vary. IBM notes that few-shot examples can help.
  • Safety and output quality: IBM notes that the model may occasionally produce inaccurate, biased, or unsafe responses and recommends pairing it with Granite Guardian. Content inside the reasoning tags is intermediate thinking and does not represent a final conclusion.
  • Coding headroom: SWE-Bench Verified reaches 47.67. Scores of 19.11 on SWE-Bench Pro and 20.56 on Terminal-Bench 2.1 show room to grow on harder agentic coding tasks.
  • Text only: The model supports text input and output, with no image processing.

Methodology Used to Evaluate the Models

This review combines independent Artificial Analysis measurements, IBM’s published results, and provider data.

Intelligence assessment

  • Models are scored on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index. It is a weighted average across agents (30%), coding (20%), scientific reasoning (20%), and general knowledge (30%).
  • Granite 4.2 8B scores 11, above the median of 8 for open-weight models of similar size.

Performance metrics

  • Time to first token (TTFT): the time between sending a request and receiving the first token of the response.
  • Output speed: the average number of tokens received per second after the first token arrives.
  • Blended pricing: a 7:2:1 ratio of cache-hit, input, and output tokens, which approximates realistic usage costs.

Benchmark datasets

IBM’s published evaluations for the 8B model, run with a framework based on the NeMo Evaluator SDK, include:

  • SWE-Bench Verified (47.67), SWE-Bench Multilingual (30.78), and SWE-Bench Pro (19.11) for software engineering
  • GPQA (64.14) and AIME 2025 (86.67) for scientific and mathematical reasoning
  • Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard v4 (52.39) and τ³-bench (58.06) for tool calling
  • IFBench (79.33) and Arena-Hard-V2 (65.19) for instruction following

IBM reports these results itself, so treat them as directional until independent evaluations catch up.

Provider comparison

  • Artificial Analysis benchmarks providers on price, output speed, and latency.
  • OpenRouter data supplies routing behavior and availability.

Key Takeaways from the Analysis

  • Strong intelligence for its size: Granite 4.2 8B scores 11 on the Intelligence Index. That is above the median of 8 for comparable open-weight models and ranks 35th of 141 models overall.
  • Cost efficiency through third-party providers: DeepInfra lists $0.06 per 1M input tokens, $0.25 per 1M output tokens, and $0.015 per 1M cached tokens. That works out to a $0.05 blended rate and about $0.02 per Intelligence Index task.
  • Apache 2.0 licensing: The permissive license allows commercial deployment, fine-tuning, and self-hosting.
  • Flexible reasoning modes: Toggling between full thinking, low-effort, and non-thinking modes lets you tune depth against latency on each query.
  • Native tool calling: Reasoning-augmented tool calling has the model weigh which tool to use before it acts. IBM reports 58.06 on τ³-bench and 52.39 on BFCL v4.
  • Competitive speed with verbose output: At 98.4 output tokens per second, the model runs faster than the median of about 75. Its verbosity still shapes total response time and cost.
  • Self-hosting is viable: IBM publishes FP8, NVFP4, MXFP4, and GGUF variants. With a capped context length, 4-bit builds fit on consumer-grade GPUs.

Conclusion

Granite 4.2 8B delivers strong reasoning in a compact, permissively licensed package. It suits organizations that want:

  • Enterprise-grade reasoning with full transparency into model weights
  • Cost-effective deployment through competitive third-party API providers
  • Agentic workflow support with native tool calling and multi-step reasoning
  • Multilingual capabilities across 12 supported languages

DeepInfra is the strongest primary API option, pairing the lowest input and cache prices with the highest measured output speed. Consider CoreWeave for output-heavy workloads and OpenRouter when automatic failover and higher availability matter most.

The model fits well-scoped tasks such as classification, metadata generation, structured API calls, document handling, and internal assistants. Human review should be part of the workflow. Demanding client-facing analysis or cutting-edge software engineering may call for a larger model.

Released by Moonshot AI on July 16, 2026, it is a 2.8 trillion parameter Mixture-of-Experts model with 104 billion […]</p>

item.title: [DeepInfra] Introducing Wan 3.0 on DeepInfra
item.content:encoded:
Introducing Wan 3.0 on DeepInfra

Published on 2026.10.19 by DeepInfra

Wan3.0 is a video generation model from Alibaba’s Wan team that combines text-to-video, image-to-video, reference-based generation, video editing, and video extension in a single model. The media you send with a request selects the workflow, so one model handles every input type.

A request can combine a text prompt with up to 20 reference assets, including images, video clips, and audio. It can also include a document or a public web page. Wan3.0 turns that input into up to 30 seconds of 1080P video with synchronized audio.

Artificial Analysis ranks Wan3.0 first on its text-to-video leaderboard with audio, at 1,173 Elo. Wan3.0 is available on DeepInfra at $0.20 per second of generated video.

What Makes This Model Different

The most distinctive design decision in Wan3.0 is its unified model. Earlier releases split these tasks across separate models, such as the Wan2.7 reference-to-video model and the Wan2.6 text-to-video model. Wan3.0 handles all of them behind one model identifier, so you manage a single endpoint as your use case changes.

Wan3.0 also doubles the maximum clip length. Alibaba lists Wan2.7 at 2 to 15 seconds per generation, while Wan3.0 reaches 30 seconds in one pass. Both earlier generations remain available on DeepInfra, including Wan2.7 reference-to-video and Wan2.6 text-to-video, each at $0.10 per second.

The supported task types are:

TaskInputNotes
Text-to-videoPrompt onlyDuration from 2 to 30 seconds
Image-to-videoFirst frame, or first and last frameAnimates the supplied image or images
Reference-to-videoImages, video clips, audio, one file, or one linkUp to 20 reference assets per request
Video editingReference video and a natural language instructionChanges visuals, plot, or dialogue without regenerating the full clip
Video extensionExisting video and a promptInput and output durations together stay within 30 seconds

The reference system accepts up to 10 reference images, 5 video clips, and 5 audio clips in one request. A request can also include one document, such as a PDF, DOCX, PPTX, or Markdown file, or one public web page. The model parses it and turns it into video.

You reference assets directly in the prompt with positional names such as Image 1 or Video 2. The numbers follow the order of the media array, and images and videos are counted separately.

Audio is on by default. The model generates dialogue, background music, and sound effects alongside the video. Set audio to false if you handle sound separately.

Output tops out at 1080P and 30 fps, with 480P and 720P tiers available. Duration can be set from 2 to 30 seconds, or set to -1 to let the model choose a length from the prompt and media.

The prompt_extend parameter defaults to true and rewrites your prompt before generation. Sparse prompts benefit most, so leave it on unless you need exact control over the wording.

Getting Started on DeepInfra

Wan3.0-Video is available on DeepInfra under the model identifier Wan-AI/Wan3.0-Video. Pricing is $0.20 per second of generated video, so a 10-second clip costs $2.00 and a full 30-second generation costs $6.00.

Billing is usage-based through a REST API that fits existing tooling. DeepInfra runs a zero-retention policy for inputs, outputs, and user data, and the platform is SOC 2 and ISO 27001 certified.

Quickstart

Create a key in the DeepInfra dashboard, then submit a text-to-video request. The response includes a video_url that points to the finished MP4.

curl -X POST "https://api.deepinfra.com/v1/inference/Wan-AI/Wan3.0-Video" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $DEEPINFRA_TOKEN" \
  -d '{
    "prompt": "A red fox running through a snowy pine forest at dusk, cinematic lighting",
    "resolution": "1080P",
    "ratio": "16:9",
    "duration": 5,
    "audio": true,
    "prompt_extend": true
  }'copy
import os
import requests
 
response = requests.post(
    "https://api.deepinfra.com/v1/inference/Wan-AI/Wan3.0-Video",
    headers={
        "Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['DEEPINFRA_TOKEN']}",
        "Content-Type": "application/json",
    },
    json={
        "prompt": "A red fox running through a snowy pine forest at dusk, cinematic lighting",
        "resolution": "1080P",
        "ratio": "16:9",
        "duration": 5,
        "audio": True,
        "prompt_extend": True,
    },
)
 
print(response.json()["video_url"])copy

Key parameters

  • duration accepts integers from 2 to 30, or -1 to let the model pick a length from your prompt and media.
  • ratio defaults to adaptive, which derives the aspect ratio from your input media. This helps most in image-to-video workflows.
  • audio defaults to true. Pass false for a silent output.
  • prompt_extend defaults to true and rewrites the prompt to improve output quality.
  • watermark defaults to false. Set it to true to add an AI-generated watermark.
  • seed accepts integers from 0 to 2,147,483,647 for reproducible outputs.
  • Reference media types cannot be combined with first_frame or last_frame in the same request.

The model page also lets you run a first generation in the browser and inspect the full parameter reference.

Conclusion

Wan3.0 removes the need to stitch together separate models for each video task. One endpoint accepts text, images, video clips, audio, documents, and web pages, and it generates synchronized audio in the same pass.

This range suits workflows that were hard to automate before. Examples include product demo videos built from a URL, story-driven clips built from a PDF script, and short-form content with consistent characters.

Start with a short 480P or 720P clip to check motion and composition, then render the final version at 1080P.

item.title: [InceptionLabs] Introducing Mercury 3|Read the blog
item.content:encoded:
Today we’re introducing Mercury 3, the most capable diffusion-based LLM released to date. Across a range of benchmarks, Mercury 3 outperforms GPT-6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5, while running 4–8x faster at 1,000+ tokens per second.

Mercury 3 demonstrates that text diffusion scales. It’s more than 40x larger than Mercury 1 and is vastly more intelligent, but just as fast.

Early-access partners already use Mercury 3 for voice and chat support, real-time tutoring, data engineering, and web navigation:

Mercury 3 at a glance

  • Quality: On par or better than frontier speed-optimized models like GPT-6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5.
  • Speed: 1,068 tokens per second on NVIDIA GPUs.
  • Context: 1M tokens, up from 260K for Mercury 2.5
  • Price: $0.20 per million input and $0.70 per million output tokens.At launch, Mercury 3 is 50% off at $0.10 per 1M input and $0.35 per 1M output. Cached tokens are 90% off the input price.

Diffusion at scale

When we launched Mercury 1, it was the first proof point that diffusion LLMs could be built for commercial applications. The open question in the AI community was whether diffusion LLMs could scale to compete with autoregressive models on complex use cases.

Mercury 3 answers that question: they can. We’ve scaled Mercury more than 40x in total parameters, and intelligence across a range of standard benchmarks has risen 3x from Mercury 1 (mini) to Mercury 3. The scaling laws that drove progress in autoregressive models hold for diffusion too.

Mercury 3 in production

Early-access partners are already running Mercury 3 to power latency-sensitive applications such as browser use agents, interactive education, real-time search agents, and customer support.

Browser Use Agents

Agents wait on the model at every step, so small delays compound quickly. Mercury keeps each pass fast, whether the agent is navigating websites, researching across sources, or analyzing logs and tracing incidents. Agents finish sooner and have time to try more approaches before answering.

We ran Mercury 3 inside our production web-agent harness against frontier models, on 50 live Mind2Web navigation tasks. Mercury 3 completed 50% of them, significantly more than GPT-6.1-Sol. It did so using the same token volume and the same number of agent steps as a frontier model, at a fraction of the per-token cost.

Shuhao Zhang, Cofounder, TinyFish AI

Interactive Education

Learning runs on fast feedback loops, and any delay pulls a student out of the material. Mercury reasons through each request and responds in near real time, whether it’s a voice tutor carrying a conversation, an assistant grading work, or an app adapting the next question to what the student just got wrong.

Mercury 3 allowed us to give every student instant feedback without giving up reasoning. Hints, marked answers and definitions now come back in about a second, with quality as good as or better than the models we ran before. When a student is stuck on a question, that speed keeps them working instead of waiting, and it was a drop-in swap for our existing stack.

Michael Tong, Co-founder/CTO, General Learning aka RevisionDojo

Real-time search agents

Search applications start to feel unresponsive after just a few seconds delay. Mercury 3 runs fast enough to process dozens of documents and still answer while the user is engaged.

On smart glasses, an answer that takes five seconds feels broken. In our Sense API tests, Octen search took about 80ms; model generation was the bottleneck. Mercury 3 delivered the best balance of speed and quality among the fast models we tested, with a median generation time of 0.9 seconds and a median end-to-end response time of 2.2 seconds.

Kuan Zou, Founder & CEO, Octen AI

Customer support

Support agents have to answer quickly, often for regulated businesses where a wrong answer is costly. Mercury keeps responses conversational without sacrificing accuracy.

At Lorikeet, we help complex and regulated businesses build a concierge for their customers that works across voice, chat and email. In chat and voice, customers need fast responses, but we can't compromise on accuracy or getting the job done correctly. In early testing, Mercury 3 beat other models on latency while also performing higher on evals and in production.

Michael Gribben, Member of Technical Staff, Lorikeet

A real-time product portfolio

Mercury 3 is the flagship model in a widening portfolio of products that enable real-time AI.

  • Mercury Voice: Mercury Voice is customized for the extreme low-latency requirements of voice applications and for minimizing time to first answer token (TTFAT), not just end-to-end latency. It’s already powering agents at Audivi AI, Altur, and OpenCall.
  • Mercury Decide: Mercury Decide is a decision model built for high-volume classification. It outperforms Jev on benchmarks including JevBench and LegalBench.

Get started

Mercury 3 is available today on the Inception API Platform and through OpenRouter, Baseten, and Vercel. It is OpenAI API compatible, so it drops into your existing stack with no rewrites. Enterprise deployments support dedicated capacity, autoscaling, compliance controls, and configurable data retention.

  • Try Mercury 3 in chat
  • Try the API with 100 million free tokens
  • Read the API docs
  • Enterprise evaluations: we'll partner with you on workload fit, eval design, and performance under your serving constraints. Contact us.

Mercury 3 is live. Diffusion scales.

item.title: [DeepInfra] Granite-4.2-8B Pricing Guide: Provider Comparison
item.content:encoded:
Granite-4.2-8B Pricing Guide: Provider Comparison

Published on 2026.10.18 by DeepInfra

Granite-4.2-8b is a practical pick for anyone shopping for a small open-weight reasoning model. It costs $0.06 per million input tokens and $0.25 per million output tokens. It also scores 11 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index among small (4B to 40B) open-weight models.

Its input price sits below the $0.12 median for comparable models, and its output price matches the $0.25 median. You can reach it directly or through routed access across multiple providers.

Granite-4.2-8b is an 8-billion-parameter reasoning model from IBM’s Granite family, released in late August 2026 and post-trained from Granite-4.1-8B-Base. It is a decoder-only dense transformer with text-in, text-out support, an Apache 2.0 license, and public weights on Hugging Face.

Developers get a 131,072-token context window, tool calling, structured JSON output, and three reasoning modes: full thinking, low-effort, and non-thinking. The mode you pick sets how much deliberation you pay for. To test locally, the quantized Granite 4.2 8B build on Ollama is a convenient starting point.

The model’s appeal comes from the shape of its tradeoff. It combines open weights, a commercial-friendly license, and long context with an Intelligence Index score of 11, ranked 35th of 141 models. Artificial Analysis also calls it somewhat verbose, which matters because output-heavy reasoning models can look cheap on input and expensive in practice.

On speed, first-token latency is competitive at 0.85 seconds against a 1.17-second median. Provider-level throughput varies, so provider choice is part of the pricing decision.

Evaluating Granite-4.2-8b comes down to one practical question: do its cost profile, 131K context window, and provider mix fit your production constraints? This guide covers DeepInfra, CoreWeave, and OpenRouter’s routing layer.

Granite-4.2-8b Executive Summary

Granite-4.2-8b is priced for cost-conscious production use. It costs $0.06/M input, $0.25/M output, and $0.015/M cached tokens on DeepInfra. OpenRouter lists the same rates on its DeepInfra route, and CoreWeave offers $0.10/M input, $0.15/M output, and $0.05/M cached tokens.

It suits teams that want an Apache 2.0 reasoning model with long context, tool calling, and flexible deployment. DeepInfra is the strongest choice for low-cost direct access, while CoreWeave and OpenRouter are the main alternatives.

Best ForProvider RecommendationWhy
Lowest price and cost-sensitive workloadsDeepInfraDeepInfra lists $0.06/M input, $0.25/M output, and $0.015/M cached tokens, the lowest input and cache prices among the providers covered.
Direct production deployment with API featuresDeepInfraIt offers public API access, zero data retention, JSON output, function calling, private endpoints, and the full 131,072-token context window.
Easiest onboarding and fastest time to first callOpenRouterOpenRouter is OpenAI-compatible and adds automatic failover plus Balanced, Nitro, Floor, and Exacto routing modes, which reduces integration and operations friction.
RAG, document-heavy, or high-throughput use casesDeepInfraArtificial Analysis measures 120 output tokens per second on DeepInfra against 89 on CoreWeave, and DeepInfra also has the lower input price.
Managed model access with reliability safeguardsOpenRouterOpenRouter lists 99.98% availability over the last 24 hours, compared with 99.03% without routing.
Tool-calling workloadsDeepInfra, or OpenRouter in Exacto modeDeepInfra lists JSON output and function calling, and OpenRouter’s Exacto mode routes for the highest tool-calling accuracy.

Understanding Tokens and How You’re Charged

Token pricing looks simple until a reasoning model writes more than you expected. Granite-4.2-8b is cheap on input and reasonable on output, but Artificial Analysis rates it somewhat verbose. Plan for that and the pricing works well. Look only at the headline input rate and the bill can surprise you.

A token is a chunk of text that can be shorter or longer than a word. Short words may be one token. Longer words, punctuation, code, and JSON structure all count too.

You are typically billed separately for:

  • tokens you send to the model
  • tokens the model generates back
  • cached prompt tokens, when a provider discounts repeated prompt prefixes
Token TypeWhat It IsWhy It Matters
Input tokensThe tokens in your prompt, system message, tool schema, chat history, and retrieved contextGranite-4.2-8b costs $0.06/M on DeepInfra. This helps with RAG, long instructions, and multi-turn agent state.
Output tokensThe tokens the model generates in its reply, including reasoning-heavy or structured responsesThis is where costs creep up. Granite-4.2-8b costs $0.25/M output on DeepInfra, and Artificial Analysis rates it somewhat verbose.
Cached tokensReused prompt tokens that a provider serves from cache at a discountUseful when you resend large system prompts, tool definitions, or repeated context. DeepInfra lists $0.015/M, a 75% discount from the base input rate.

For Granite-4.2-8b, the practical billing pattern looks like this:

  • Long prompts are relatively cheap.
  • Long answers matter more.
  • Reused prompt prefixes are where caching pays off.

Artificial Analysis reports a blended rate of $0.05 per 1M tokens, using a 7:2:1 cache-hit, input, and output mix. This blended rate only applies if your traffic follows that mix.

  • If your app produces long reasoning traces, verbose tool arguments, or bulky JSON, your real cost skews closer to output pricing.
  • If your app repeatedly sends the same system prompt, tool schema, and document boilerplate, cache discounts do real work.

Provider Token-Cost Tradeoffs for Granite-4.2-8b

Provider choice changes the shape of your bill. DeepInfra is cheaper on input and cache, while CoreWeave is cheaper on output.

ProviderInputOutputCacheToken-Cost AdvantageToken-Cost Downside
DeepInfra$0.06/M$0.25/M$0.015/MBest fit for prompt-heavy workloads, RAG, long context, and reusable prompt prefixesHigher output price, so verbose generations can erase the cheap-input advantage
OpenRouter via DeepInfra route$0.06/M$0.25/M$0.015/MSame token economics as DeepInfra, plus routing convenienceSame output-cost profile as DeepInfra
CoreWeave via OpenRouter$0.10/M$0.15/M$0.05/MBetter fit for output-heavy workloads, especially when the model reasons at lengthInput and cache cost more, so large prompts and repeated context add up
OpenRouter auto-routing$0.06 to $0.10/M$0.15 to $0.25/M$0.015 to $0.05/MFailover and routing modes, including Floor for the cheapest providerCost depends on which provider serves each request

The practical split looks like this:

  • Choose DeepInfra if your app sends a lot of tokens into the model.
  • Choose CoreWeave if your app gets a lot of tokens back from the model.
  • Choose OpenRouter routing if you want operational flexibility and can accept variable per-request pricing.

Speed adds a second factor. Artificial Analysis measures 120 output tokens per second on DeepInfra and 89 on CoreWeave. A 500-token response takes 21.69 seconds on DeepInfra and 28.72 seconds on CoreWeave. Time to first chunk is close, at 0.77 and 0.74 seconds.

Benchmarked verbosity makes output cost a budgeting issue. Artificial Analysis measured 130M output tokens across its Intelligence Index runs, against an 82M median for comparable models. Price this model on more than input cost.

A few concrete patterns:

  • RAG over long documents: DeepInfra usually has the cleaner cost profile because input and cache are cheap.
  • Structured extraction with short answers: DeepInfra still tends to win because output stays bounded.
  • Reasoning assistant with long responses: CoreWeave can be cheaper overall despite the higher input rate, though its measured output speed is lower.
  • Agent workflows with repeated tool schemas and stable system prompts: DeepInfra benefits more from low cache pricing.
  • Router-based deployments: OpenRouter can send traffic to either provider, so monitor the actual provider mix instead of trusting the top-line listing.

The safest way to estimate Granite-4.2-8b cost is to model three separate numbers:

  • average input tokens per request
  • average output tokens per request
  • cache hit rate on repeated prompt prefixes

Skip the output estimate and the model can surprise you. Skip cache behavior and you can misprice repeated-agent workloads by a wide margin.

DeepInfra: Best Fit for Prompt-Heavy Workloads

DeepInfra is the lowest-cost option for running Granite-4.2-8b at production scale. The company says it built its service from the ground up, from GPU hardware to the API layer. That ownership gives it control over cost, performance, and reliability.

With this model, DeepInfra pairs low token pricing with practical deployment features: public API access, zero data retention, JSON output, function calling, and private endpoints.

Model NameBest Use CaseContext WindowInput (per 1M)Output (per 1M)
Granite-4.2-8bCost-efficient reasoning, tool use, and long-context API workloads131,072 tokens$0.06$0.25

DeepInfra lists Granite-4.2-8b at $0.06 per 1M input tokens and $0.25 per 1M output tokens. This makes it an efficient option for teams optimizing token spend, especially on prompt-heavy and repeated-context workloads. DeepInfra also offers $0.015 per 1M cached tokens.

If you expect meaningful volume, DeepInfra is the provider to shortlist first for Granite-4.2-8b.

Real-World Cost Scenarios for Developers

Each scenario below runs Granite-4.2-8b on DeepInfra and compares CoreWeave at its listed rates. DeepInfra is strongest when a workload is prompt-heavy, context-heavy, or cache-friendly.

Scenario 1: RAG support assistant over large internal docs

You are building a developer-facing support bot that searches internal runbooks, SDK docs, incident notes, and architecture pages before answering. Each request carries a large prompt with retrieved context, while the answer stays moderate. RAG workloads spend more on input than on output, so low input pricing matters most.

VolumeModelProviderInput TokensOutput TokensMonthly Cost
10M tokens/monthGranite-4.2-8bDeepInfra8M2M$0.98

Cost math:

  • Input: 8M × $0.06/M = $0.48
  • Output: 2M × $0.25/M = $0.50
  • Total: $0.98/month

The same workload on CoreWeave costs $1.10/month, so DeepInfra is cheaper by $0.12.

Scenario 2: Agent workflow with repeated tool schemas and cached system prompts

You are shipping an internal coding or ops agent that sends the same system prompt, tool definitions, and response schema on every call. DeepInfra’s $0.015/M cached rate makes those repeated prefixes much cheaper than normal input tokens.

IBM says the Granite 4.2 models think about which tool to call, and why, before making the call. That behavior suits agent workflows with stable scaffolding.

VolumeModelProviderInput TokensOutput TokensMonthly Cost
10M tokens/monthGranite-4.2-8bDeepInfra2M input + 7M cached1M$0.48

Cost math:

  • Input: 2M × $0.06/M = $0.12
  • Cached: 7M × $0.015/M = $0.105
  • Output: 1M × $0.25/M = $0.25
  • Total: $0.475, or $0.48/month rounded

The same token mix on CoreWeave costs $0.70/month ($0.20 input, $0.35 cached, and $0.15 output), so DeepInfra is cheaper by about $0.23.

Scenario 3: Long-context document triage with short structured outputs

Suppose you process product specs, contracts, tickets, or compliance documents. You ask Granite-4.2-8b to return compact JSON, such as classifications, extracted fields, risk flags, or summaries. The model reads a lot and writes a little. You get its long context window and structured output support without paying a premium to send large inputs.

VolumeModelProviderInput TokensOutput TokensMonthly Cost
50M tokens/monthGranite-4.2-8bDeepInfra45M5M$3.95

Cost math:

  • Input: 45M × $0.06/M = $2.70
  • Output: 5M × $0.25/M = $1.25
  • Total: $3.95/month

The same workload on CoreWeave costs $5.25/month, so DeepInfra is cheaper by $1.30.

Scenario 4: Multi-turn app with persistent conversation state

You are building a multilingual assistant where each turn includes prior chat state, policy instructions, and retrieved snippets. Granite-4.2-8b supports 12 languages, and low input pricing keeps repeated context affordable. This works best when answers stay short while the prompt grows over time.

VolumeModelProviderInput TokensOutput TokensMonthly Cost
20M tokens/monthGranite-4.2-8bDeepInfra16M4M$1.96

Cost math:

  • Input: 16M × $0.06/M = $0.96
  • Output: 4M × $0.25/M = $1.00
  • Total: $1.96/month

The same workload on CoreWeave costs $2.20/month, so DeepInfra is cheaper by $0.24.

Scenario 5: Cheap experimentation before private deployment

Many developers start with prototyping rather than volume. Granite-4.2-8b on DeepInfra lets you test tool calling, JSON output, and long prompts through a public API. You can move to private endpoints with zero data retention later. A small token budget covers meaningful experiments.

VolumeModelProviderInput TokensOutput TokensMonthly Cost
5M tokens/monthGranite-4.2-8bDeepInfra4M1M$0.49

Cost math:

  • Input: 4M × $0.06/M = $0.24
  • Output: 1M × $0.25/M = $0.25
  • Total: $0.49/month

The same workload on CoreWeave costs $0.55/month, so DeepInfra is cheaper by $0.06.

What These Scenarios Show

The pattern holds across all five scenarios:

  • DeepInfra is the best fit when Granite-4.2-8b reads more than it writes.
  • It gets better when you can reuse prompt prefixes and benefit from $0.015/M cached tokens.
  • It is especially attractive for: RAG extraction pipelines multi-turn assistants tool-using agents with stable schemas early-stage prototyping that may later need private deployment

If large prompts, repeated context, and controlled output length dominate your workload, DeepInfra offers the cleanest cost profile of the providers covered here.

Conclusion

Choosing a provider for Granite-4.2-8b comes down to where your token spend lives. The model is inexpensive to feed and reasonably priced on output. Its measured verbosity makes the output side of the bill matter more than the headline input rate suggests.

Get that ratio wrong and the provider that looks cheapest on paper can cost more in practice.

Prompt-heavy and cache-friendly workloads fit DeepInfra’s $0.06/M input and $0.015/M cached rates best. Examples include RAG pipelines, tool-calling agents with stable schemas, and document extraction.

If your workload is output-heavy and the model reasons at length, model CoreWeave’s lower $0.15/M output rate against your actual token ratios. Weigh its lower measured output speed too. If operational flexibility matters, OpenRouter’s routing layer adds failover and higher reported availability.

The practical checklist is short: estimate your average input length, estimate your average output length, and decide whether reusable prompt prefixes can earn cache discounts. Those three numbers predict your monthly cost better than any blended benchmark rate.

Granite-4.2-8b’s Apache 2.0 license and public weights keep you free of any single provider. Starting on a managed API and migrating later is a real option. The Granite 4.2 8B chat completions API reference covers integration details.

Run a few representative requests through DeepInfra’s API, measure your actual token ratios, and build from there. The entry cost is low enough that the experiment is cheap.
