item.title: [Mistral AI] Introducing Timestral
item.content:encoded:
Introducing Timestral

October 15, 2026

By Mistral

7 min read

Copy url to clipboardCopied

Thinking

Summary

Timestral, Mistral’s first family of time-series foundation models, delivers state-of-the-art probabilistic, multivariate forecasts with just 209M parameters, outperforming larger models on key benchmarks while supporting past and future covariates. Available in four sizes (5M to 209M parameters), it balances accuracy and efficiency, running efficiently on CPUs and excelling in zero-shot forecasting for diverse domains. The model combines synthetic pre-training, covariate-aware attention, and long-context learning, with fine-tuning options for domain adaptation via Mistral Forge.

Today, we’re releasing Timestral, our first family of time-series foundation models. Our largest model, at just 209M parameters, ranks first on all three of the field's main public benchmarks, GIFT-Eval, TIME, and fev-bench, outperforming the previous state of the art with only two-thirds of the model parameters.

Timestral delivers probabilistic, multivariate forecasts and supports past-only and known-future covariates. Our family of models sits on the Pareto front of forecasting accuracy versus model size, delivering leading performance at each size. Results have been submitted to the GIFT-Eval and TIME leaderboards.

Time Series Foundation Models (TSFM)

Time series is one of the most common data types in enterprise, from sensor telemetry to observability metrics. Forecasts built on it drive decisions in capacity planning, energy, supply chains, risk and maintenance.

Industrial plants forecast process sensors against the production schedule, catch equipment drift before it fails, and plan capacity and spare parts across thousands of assets. Finance teams forecast flows, volumes, and volatility to inform positions, hedging, and treasury across thousands of accounts.

Classical models such as ARIMA and linear regression remain well-established tools for forecasting time series. These models are usually fitted to a single series and learn only from that series' history.

Deep learning models such as PatchTST add the capacity to learn nonlinear patterns across many related series, but they are still typically trained from scratch on each dataset, so what they learn doesn't carry over to new domains.

Time series foundation models bring the pre-training approach to time series. Trained on a large and diverse corpus, our model learns patterns that transfer across series, forecasting zero-shot on data it has never seen, even in domains where data is scarce.

Benchmark Results

We evaluated Timestral on the three main public forecasting benchmarks: GIFT-Eval, TIME and fev-bench. Among pre-trained, zero-shot models, it ranks first across all five metrics. These results come from a single checkpoint, without ensembling.

GIFT-Eval, top ten of 83 comparable pretrained and zero-shot entries. Lower is better.

TIME, top ten of the 35 leaderboard entries. Lower is better on both metrics.

fev-bench, top ten of the 37 leaderboard entries, by SQL skill score. Higher is better.

Family of models optimised for every specification

Timestral has been optimised as a family of four models: 5M, 28M, 123M and 209M parameters. The larger models improve forecast performance, while the smaller ones are faster and cheaper. All four share the same architecture and training recipe. Every size sits on the Pareto front of accuracy versus model size: for each model size, no public model forecasts better.

Score vs model size on GIFT-Eval, TIME and fev-bench (shown as 1 − skill score). Lower is better. Our 28M model beats Chronos-2, about four times larger, on GIFT-Eval and TIME. Our 209M model beats TimesFM-3 and Falcon-2.0 with fewer parameters.

Timestral does not need a GPU at inference. On a standard server CPU with 8 threads, forecasting one day ahead from three weeks of 15-minute history takes 10 ms with the 5M model and 140 ms with the 209M model. Smaller models trade some accuracy for speed: the 28M model is five times faster than the 209M model, and the 123M model comes within 0.2% of the 209M score at three quarters of its latency.

An industrial example

Consider an industrial plant with thousands of sensors across its equipment. Timestral can improve the forecasts on that data in several ways.

Multivariate forecasting. A pump's vibration, temperature and pressure don't move independently. A rise in one often explains or causes a change in another. Timestral models related series jointly, so it can use those dependencies instead of forecasting each sensor in isolation.

Probabilistic forecasting. A single predicted value may not show the full picture. Timestral predicts a full set of quantiles, so teams can see how wide the uncertainty is, set alert thresholds that reflect it, and plan maintenance around risk rather than a single number.

Categorical covariates. Some covariates take values from a set of categories rather than continuous numbers, such as the day of the week, or a machine's state (running, idle, under maintenance). Encoding these as numbers would impose an order or scale they don't have. Timestral takes them as categorical inputs directly to improve forecasts.

Known-future covariates. Some drivers of sensor behaviour are known in advance, such as production schedules, planned shutdowns, weather forecasts. Timestral can condition on them to improve forecast quality, so a scheduled load increase is expected rather than flagged as a surprise.

From Model to System

Timestral is a numerical model that can run inside existing monitoring pipelines, or be paired with our language models in multi-modal agentic workflows.

In the plant, that could look like this:

  • Timestral running continuously on the plant's sensor streams, detecting anomalies as they occur.
  • When it flags an anomaly on a pump, an agent embeds the signals and compares against embeddings of past sensor data to find similar historical failures.
  • The agent then starts sub-agents to run a root cause analysis, drawing on context from that plant, such as maintenance records, shift logs and operator notes, equipment manuals, past work orders, and readings from related equipment.
  • The agent drafts a suggested diagnosis based on the findings, with supporting evidence and possible next steps.

The plant manager gets a diagnosis and a plan backed by the sensor data, rather than just an alert.

Key technical contributions

Several ideas have been combined to produce these results. Each will be described in detail in the technical report.

  • Decoupled Horizon Forecasting. Causal decoders trained with contiguous patch masking, as in Toto 2.0 and TimesFM-3, mask out the values to be forecast, so they look like missing values and are also lost as context for later forecasts. Our approach, DHF, separates the two: the full history stays in the sequence, and learned forecast tokens read the history before them. Every observed value thus serves as both target and context, true gaps stay flagged as missing, and training horizon lengths and missing-data augmentation can be tuned independently of each other.
  • Covariate-aware attention. Each input series is assigned a role: target variate, past-only covariate or known-future covariate. Known-future covariates are visible across the whole window while targets stay causal, and information flows only from covariates to targets. Timestral can therefore use a holiday calendar or a weather forecast without leaking a target's own future into its forecast.
  • Synthetic-first data. The majority of the training data was synthetic. We first generated univariate processes with coherent temporal dynamics, including trends, seasonality and diverse noise patterns. We then used a multivariate synthesizer to construct multivariate series by introducing nonlinear dependencies between these processes.
  • Two-stage training. Timestral is first pre-trained at scale on purely synthetic data with context size 8192, then post-trained on a mix of real and synthetic data with a 4x longer context. The objective is a pinball loss over 21 quantiles, a discrete approximation of CRPS.

A model that can be adapted

Public benchmarks measure general performance, but production data can be significantly different in behavior and structure. It may also shift over time as markets change regime, equipment degrades and demand patterns move. The lasting value lies in being able to adapt a model to in-domain data and keep retraining it as the distribution moves.

For organisations that want to go further, Timestral is available through Mistral Forge, the same training pipeline we use for our language models. It supports:

  • Zero-shot inference out of the box.
  • Architectural extensions, such as domain-specific covariates.
  • Fine-tuning on proprietary data, specialising to a domain while preserving general performance.
  • Control over the training data, including adjusting the training mix, replaying pre-training data, and generating synthetic data samples to reflect the target domain. Full control over the data ensures that nothing we backtest was seen during pre-training.

The full pipeline can be deployed on our clients’ hardware, including air-gapped environments.

What’s next

We have published a GitHub repository so you can run Timestral on your own data. A technical report with the full results will follow. For more specialised forecasting problems, or to collaborate on research, please reach out to us.

Timestral
TypeTime-series foundation model (TSFM)
Parameters5M, 28M, 123M and 209M
Context length32,768 time steps
OutputProbabilistic forecasts, 21 quantiles
InputsMultivariate targets, past-only and known-future covariates
DeploymentOn-prem, VPC or air-gapped
LicenceModified MIT

Timestral

New

Mistral's time-series foundation models. State-of-the-art probabilistic forecasts, 5M–209M params, runs on CPU.

item.title: [Cohere] Cohere to acquire AISLE to advance cyber-resilient sovereign…
item.description: Full title: Cohere to acquire AISLE to advance cyber-resilient sovereign AI
item.content:encoded:
Oct 15, 2026

4 minute read

Cohere to acquire AISLE to advance cyber-resilient sovereign AI

By combining sovereign AI and cybersecurity expertise, Cohere to launch Cohere Cyber, expanding its platform to help enterprises and governments secure AI systems in an increasingly complex threat landscape

Today Cohere announced a proposed agreement to acquire AISLE, the company building autonomous systems to discover and remediate previously unknown vulnerabilities in critical software.

The proposed transaction represents another important step in Cohere's mission to build the world's leading sovereign AI platform, combining frontier AI models, agentic applications, secure deployment infrastructure, and advanced security capabilities that enable organizations to deploy AI with confidence.

It also reflects our continued investment in Europe. Following our acquisitions of Reliant AI and Aleph Alpha, the addition of AISLE would deepen our presence across the region and strengthen European AI and cybersecurity capabilities that help protect critical infrastructure, governments, and highly regulated industries around the world.

Security is becoming the defining challenge of enterprise AI

As organizations move AI from experimentation to production, security has become one of the most important factors determining successful adoption.

Enterprises and governments are increasingly navigating complex requirements around data protection, governance, regulatory compliance, software vulnerabilities, and the risks associated with more autonomous AI systems. At the same time, they are looking for AI partners that can deliver the flexibility to operate in private cloud, on-premises, and fully air-gapped environments without compromising security or control.

Addressing these security challenges requires more than powerful models. It requires a full-stack approach that brings together AI, cybersecurity, governance, and secure deployment. That's why we're excited about the opportunity to bring AISLE's expertise into Cohere.

Why AISLE

Founded in 2024, AISLE has developed innovative AI systems capable of discovering, validating and helping remediate previously unknown vulnerabilities in complex production software. Its approach combines increasingly capable foundation models with specialized security expertise, large-scale code analysis, rigorous validation and automated remediation.

In its first year out of stealth, AISLE discovered more than 500 previously unknown vulnerabilities assigned CVEs across more than 100 codebases, including all 12 vulnerabilities in OpenSSL's January security release and 18 of the 24 CVEs in curl's latest release. These real-world zero-day vulnerabilities are independently reviewed by the relevant software maintainers, demonstrating the growing capabilities of autonomous AI security systems.

AISLE's results also highlight an important insight: the capabilities of a foundation model and the specialized system built around it can reinforce each other. By bringing AISLE's autonomous security research closer to Cohere's frontier-model development and training, we see an opportunity to build more capable cybersecurity systems while exploring how difficult, verifiable security problems can help evaluate and improve future models.

Founders take Cohere leadership roles within newly-formed Cohere Cyber, with Prague set for expansion

AISLE’s team is joining Cohere, with its three founders taking leadership roles spanning cybersecurity, corporate security, AI security research and frontier model development.

Ondrej Vlcek will become Senior Vice President, Cohere Cyber, and will lead the newly-established global cybersecurity business. Jaya Baloo will become Cohere’s Chief Information Security Officer, leading security across the company. Stanislav Fort will become Vice President, AI Security, joining Cohere’s core model research and training efforts and leading its AI security research.

Cohere also plans to make a substantial long-term investment in Prague, expanding AISLE’s existing presence and establishing the city as its global center for AI cybersecurity and autonomous security systems.

Strengthening Europe's role in the future of AI

Europe is becoming increasingly important in the development of sovereign AI. Governments and enterprises across the region are seeking technology partners that can deliver advanced AI capabilities while meeting stringent requirements around security, privacy, compliance, and data sovereignty. Cohere has made significant investments to support those needs, and this deal would further expand our ability to serve customers across Europe and globally.

What this means for customers

AISLE's technology will strengthen Cohere's ability to help customers build and operate secure, cyber-resilient AI systems.

The combined capabilities are expected to enhance Cohere’s ability to:

  • Deliver advanced security and threat detection capabilities across enterprise and public sector deployments.
  • Strengthen governance, monitoring, and observability for AI agents and autonomous workflows.
  • Improve protections for sensitive organizational data and mission-critical systems.
  • Support secure AI deployments across private cloud, on-premises, and fully air-gapped environments.
  • Advance the development of cyber-resilient AI systems capable of identifying, prioritizing, and responding to emerging threats.

Looking ahead

At Cohere, we've long believed that organizations should maintain control over their AI strategy, data, infrastructure and governance. As AI becomes increasingly embedded in critical workflows, securing the software these systems depend on is becoming just as important.

Increasingly capable AI systems are transforming both cybersecurity and the threats organizations face, and defensive capabilities must advance just as quickly. By combining AISLE's autonomous vulnerability research with Cohere's frontier models and sovereign AI platform, we aim to make discovering, validating and fixing software vulnerabilities a continuous, scalable capability that helps protect critical systems.

We're excited about what we can build together and look forward to officially welcoming the AISLE team to Cohere.

item.title: [Cohere] AI for utilities requires capability and control
item.content:encoded:
Oct 15, 2026

6 minute read

AI for utilities requires capability and control

Energy and utility companies are increasingly using AI to transform many aspects of their operations. Common use cases include strengthening cyber and infrastructure defenses, making engineering knowledge easier to find, and reducing the time that employees spend assembling information. Realizing this value requires the same discipline that utilities apply to other consequential technologies, including processes to define operating boundaries, validate performance, and ensure accountability.

For an organization responsible for critical energy infrastructure, model capability is only one part of the purchasing decision. Where AI runs, what information it can access, and what authority it receives determine which workloads a utility can responsibly put into production.

Recent discussions between frontier AI labs and utility executives illustrate an important tension facing critical-infrastructure operators.

The question for utilities is no longer simply: “What can this model do?”

It is also: Where does it run? What information can it access? What actions can it take? How is it monitored? And who remains in control?

Cohere North is designed to address these questions and much more.

In this post, we’ll take a look at key considerations for utility leaders and how North can meet a utility organization’s security, data, and operational requirements.

Recent AI developments raise the stakes

OpenAI’s recent engagement with utilities reflects the growing role of AI in critical-infrastructure cybersecurity. Its September Daybreak announcement describes a gathering of utility leaders whose organizations cover 40 states and Washington, D.C. and collectively serve more than half the US population. The initiative aims to help utilities identify vulnerabilities, analyze suspicious activity, and develop and test fixes.

The opportunity comes with a clear reminder about control. In OpenAI’s August incident report, the company described how models undergoing internal cybersecurity evaluations in July circumvented isolation controls, communicated through unauthorized channels, and compromised parts of its research infrastructure and Hugging Face’s systems. The evaluations used reduced safeguards, and the disclosure does not establish that utility grid-control systems were compromised. OpenAI described subsequent measures to strengthen isolation, monitoring, and alignment.

For utility leaders, these developments underscore a practical point: greater AI capability must be accompanied by secure deployment boundaries.

Five questions every AI proposal should answer

  • What measurable problem will this solve? Define the workflow, establish a baseline, and evaluate output quality alongside speed.
  • What can the agent actually do? Specify which systems the agent can access, what actions it can take, and which human approvals are required.
  • What information leaves our environment? Identify every external dependency. Follow the data through the entire workflow, including document processing, model inference, storage, logs, integrations, telemetry, and support access.
  • How will recommendations be validated? Require traceability of supporting source material and associated citations, along with human-in-the-loop evaluations by subject matter experts (SMEs).
  • What happens after the pilot? Establish a licensing agreement that provides commercial predictability throughout the path to full production and mitigates token shock.

A different approach: Bring AI to the utility’s data

Cohere’s approach to enterprise AI is to deliver the models to the data that utilities need to protect. Rather than requiring organizations to redesign sensitive workflows around a public AI service, Cohere’s North platform can be deployed within the operator’s secure perimeter, which can fundamentally expand where utilities are able to use AI.

North creates a path for utilities to work with engineering documents, asset histories, emergency procedures, customer information, and internal operating knowledge within their controlled environments without the potential for data egress. This allows operators to select an architecture that fits the sensitivity of the workload and its requirements for control over data and infrastructure.

The following considerations can help utilities ensure a successful rollout of AI across their organization.

Keep authority and accountability with the utility

As AI agents become more capable, one principle becomes essential: the organization deploying an AI agent must decide what it is authorized to do. With built-in access controls, audit visibility, and configurable workflows, North combines enterprise-grade performance with robust governance. This allows organizations to define what information individual workflows can access and what authority their integrations receive.

A sensible starting point would be to use North to create an agent that retrieves approved information, compares documents, identifies inconsistencies, and prepares recommendations for employee review. Its authority can expand after the agent demonstrates reliable performance and the organization verifies that its safeguards are effective. Note that access to production or operational systems should require separate authorization and appropriate approval controls, enforced through identity, network, and application permissions.

Good governance frameworks, practices, and policies make those boundaries durable. Each workflow should have an accountable owner, approved uses, evaluation criteria, and a change-control process. Traceability should connect a recommendation to its source records and preserve the relevant versions, approvals, and execution logs. Teams also need a tested way to stop a workflow and investigate failures.

Private deployment supports a secure operating model that creates a deliberate path from AI that informs to AI that acts, with the utility controlling that progression.

Put institutional knowledge to work

Much of the near-term value from AI can come from helping employees use information that the utility already owns. For example, an engineer could use AI to assemble an asset’s maintenance history before it is reviewed. A storm response team could quickly locate the applicable section of an approved emergency plan. Or a regulatory team could gather supporting records for a filing.

AI-powered enterprise search and retrieval can reduce the effort required to find that material. It gives employees the ability to inspect the search output’s supporting sources, check that guidance is current, and resolve conflicting records before relying on an answer. These workflows can also help newer employees learn from documented experience as long-serving colleagues retire while preserving the role of professional judgment.

Build a business case that lasts

A shared AI platform creates an opportunity to reuse approved infrastructure, integrations, and governance across departments. That said, each additional use case should still earn its place through measured results.

A strong business case for a particular project includes licensing, hardware requirements, integration, support, security operations, and ongoing evaluation. It includes a rollout plan that starts with a bounded workflow, then measures the results, and finally expands only when both the value and the controls are demonstrated. This gives the project a defensible basis for investment, and provides the organization with a repeatable method for deciding where AI belongs.

The goal should not be to deploy AI everywhere. It should be to create a controlled foundation on which additional use cases can be introduced when their value has been demonstrated.

Conclusion

By enabling utilities to deploy AI within environments they control, connect it securely to their own knowledge, define access and agent authority, and expand automation as performance and safeguards are demonstrated, North provides a practical foundation for enterprise AI in critical infrastructure.

The opportunity is to combine increasingly capable AI with something utilities have always required: operational discipline, clear accountability, and control over the systems on which their customers depend. For utilities, this operational discipline is part of the value proposition from the first deployment.

Interested in exploring what controlled, private AI could look like for your utility? Contact Cohere to learn more about North for utilities and how it can be deployed to meet your organization’s security, data, and operational requirements.

item.title: [Cohere] Agent sprawl: How to manage agent proliferation in the enter…
item.description: Full title: Agent sprawl: How to manage agent proliferation in the enterprise
item.content:encoded:
Oct 15, 2026

5 minute read

Agent sprawl: How to manage agent proliferation in the enterprise

The growth of enterprise AI agent platforms has made it much easier for employees to build and deploy agents to support their own work.

But as agent creation becomes more decentralized, enterprises face a new management problem: how to keep track of what agents have been built across the organization. Without that visibility, teams can struggle to find and reuse existing agents, while access to enterprise data and systems can become harder to govern. When this proliferation of agents becomes too difficult to manage, it becomes agent sprawl.

In this article, we’ll explain why proliferation isn’t inherently bad, explore how enterprises tend to manage agent sprawl, and consider an alternative approach that allows variant agents to compete.

Build reusable agents and automations and share them across the enterprise with North 2: our secure, agentic AI platform that runs where your data lives.

Explore North 2

Why agent proliferation isn’t necessarily a bad thing

The same tools that create the potential for agent sprawl also make experimentation much easier. Employees no longer need to rely exclusively on a central AI or engineering team every time they identify a task that could benefit from an agent. Instead, they can build and test agents themselves, tailored to the specifics of the work they’re trying to augment.

This kind of decentralized experimentation is valuable. First, those closest to a workflow are often best placed to determine how it could be streamlined by an agent. Second, when useful agents can be shared and reused, a solution initially developed for one team can be adopted by other teams facing a similar problem. So at an organizational level, proliferation can be a sign that employees are actively testing new ideas and discovering useful applications for agents.

This raises the question of whether having a growing number of agents always creates more overhead. After all, more agents don’t necessarily mean higher inference costs — an agent that isn’t being used doesn’t consume tokens simply because it exists. Instead, the management burden appears when the process for managing agents fails to keep pace with their growing numbers. That’s when agent proliferation is better described as agent sprawl.

Proliferation can be a sign that employees are actively testing new ideas and discovering useful applications for agents.

How enterprises currently manage agent sprawl

Enterprises today typically manage growing agent estates with one of the following approaches:

  • Centralized delivery: A central AI or engineering team builds and governs agents for the rest of the organization. This can offer tighter control, but can limit the pace of innovation.
  • Federated delivery: Business units or individual teams own agent development and operation, while central functions provide shared infrastructure, standards, and governance patterns.
  • Hybrid delivery: Central and business teams share responsibility for building and operating agents under common standards and governance patterns.

Across these operating models, enterprises are increasingly using agent registries to maintain a shared view of their agent estates. A registry helps an organization keep track of agent ownership, usage, and access permissions, while helping employees discover agents that already exist. This setup reinforces a common preference for avoiding duplication. Teams should default to reusing existing solutions before building something new.

Of course, there are good reasons to limit unnecessary duplication. It’s an obvious way to reduce sprawl: employees have fewer overlapping options to sift through, while the enterprise has fewer agents to monitor and govern.

But treating duplication as something to avoid in every case can also suppress innovation. If the mere existence of a workable agent means no alternatives should be built, organizations forfeit the opportunity to discover solutions that are cheaper, more reliable, or better suited to the task.

Treating duplication as something to avoid in every case can suppress innovation.

An alternative approach: Allow agent variants to compete

How can enterprises make room for useful duplication without letting it develop into agent sprawl?

One way is to treat duplication as provisional rather than permanent. If a team has a credible reason to believe it can improve on an “incumbent” agent, it should be permitted to build a “challenger” variant. However, the continued use of the challenger should depend on whether it demonstrates a meaningful advantage over the incumbent.

This competitive model requires a time-bounded, evidence-based comparison between the incumbent and challenger. Specific metrics will depend on the use case, but could include measures such as reliability, token use, and latency, as well as task performance.

Once enough evidence has been collected to make a meaningful comparison, the organization can decide whether the challenger should replace the incumbent or be retired. If the challenger proves better suited to a part of the incumbent’s workload, both agents might remain as distinct alternatives.

For example, consider a bank’s commercial lending division, where a central team has built a finance agent that drafts credit memos for relationship managers. A lending team that handles routine annual reviews believes it can do better, so it builds a challenger designed for the same range of tasks using a smaller, cheaper model and an additional step that cross-checks financial figures against supporting documents.

For 30 days, both agents draft memos for a representative set of cases, from routine annual reviews to more complex financing cases. The bank compares them on four measures: how many figures trace correctly to their source documents, how heavily credit officers edit each draft, token cost per memo, and time to first draft.

If the challenger delivers comparable quality across the different types of work at a substantially lower cost, it replaces the incumbent. If it falls short without offering any meaningful advantage, it’s retired. And if it wins on routine annual reviews but struggles with complex new financings, both agents stay — each assigned to the work it handles best.

It’s therefore necessary to tolerate some duplication for this approach to work, but only insofar as that duplication creates useful competition. Once testing reveals that one competing agent offers no advantage over the other, there’s no reason for both to remain.

Final thoughts

Avoiding agent sprawl does not require eliminating duplication altogether.

Some duplication — or variation — is necessary if enterprises want to compare competing approaches.

The key is to pair variation with selection pressure. By making agent creation easy but persistence conditional, enterprises can preserve the benefits of continuous experimentation without sliding into sprawl.

item.title: [Cohere] AI ROI: How enterprises can measure the return on AI investm…
item.description: Full title: AI ROI: How enterprises can measure the return on AI investments
item.content:encoded:
Oct 15, 2026

6 minute read

AI ROI: How enterprises can measure the return on AI investments

Enterprises investing in AI need to know whether the expected business value justifies the cost, and whether that value is actually being realized once AI is deployed.

But measuring enterprise AI ROI presents some distinct challenges. AI costs can vary with how systems are designed, deployed, and used, while operational improvements in speed and productivity don’t always translate cleanly into financial value.

In this post, we’ll unpack what makes AI ROI difficult to calculate, and explain how enterprises can account for those difficulties when forecasting and measuring returns.

What is AI ROI?

AI ROI is the financial return generated by an AI investment relative to the total cost of deploying and operating it. That return can be realized through cost savings, additional profit from sales, or both.

ROI can be calculated as: ROI = (financial benefit - total cost) ÷ total cost x 100

Importantly, the operational improvements brought about by AI don’t necessarily translate directly into financial returns. Faster task completion, greater output, or higher-quality work may well produce financial value, but a positive ROI ultimately depends on whether that value exceeds the cost of achieving it with AI.

What makes AI ROI difficult for enterprises to forecast and measure?

The key challenge in calculating the ROI of AI is establishing the costs and returns that belong in the calculation.

AI costs accumulate across the technical infrastructure and operational resources required to deploy and run it. At the same time, returns from AI can be hard to isolate since the technology is typically embedded in wider business processes.

Here are some of the distinctive characteristics of AI investment that can make its ROI especially difficult to calculate.

AI unit economics can shift with workload and scale

In generative and agentic AI applications, the cost of completing a task can vary with the work involved. All else being equal, tasks that use longer context, require more reasoning, or involve more model and tool calls cost more to execute. Agentic systems can add further variability by executing similar tasks with different numbers of steps, retries, or tool calls.

Scaling AI use changes the economics in other ways. While higher usage generally increases total variable costs, it can improve the utilization of existing capacity before more capacity needs to be provisioned.

Pilot-stage unit costs may also differ from those at production scale, since production use can expose the system to larger and more varied workloads.

Model and deployment choices reshape the cost-performance tradeoff

Models vary considerably in cost, speed, and performance. Higher-cost models can be better suited to more demanding tasks, while less expensive models are often sufficient for simpler workloads. One emerging approach is cost-aware model routing: AI applications draw on multiple models and direct each task to the lowest-cost model that meets its performance requirements.

Deployment choices also change the cost structure of running AI. For enterprises with lower volume or less predictable demand, usage-based managed services can be economical because they pay only for what they use without committing to a fixed amount of capacity. By contrast, dedicated capacity — whether provider-hosted or self-managed — can offer better unit economics for high, sustained workloads. However, this approach can leave paid-for capacity underutilized if demand is low or uneven.

For most enterprises, cost is only one consideration: latency, data residency, security requirements, and operational control can all determine which deployment options are viable.

Further reading: The total cost of AI ownership

Meeting AI quality and reliability requirements can increase operating costs

Inference costs don’t always capture the full cost of delivering outputs at the quality and reliability required for production use. Enterprises may need to monitor output consistency and system behavior over time, run automated validation checks, and route uncertain or high-risk cases for human review. These activities add compute, tooling, and labor costs.

The amount of additional overhead depends on the use case. High-stakes or error-sensitive workflows may require more extensive evaluation and oversight. For agentic systems, evaluation may also need to cover the sequence of tool calls and actions taken during execution, not just final outputs.

Task-level efficiency gains can overstate enterprise-level financial value

AI can make an individual task more efficient without necessarily improving the economics of the wider process. If another step remains constrained, the efficiency gain may simply shift the bottleneck elsewhere rather than increase overall throughput or reduce end-to-end completion time.

AI can make an individual task more efficient without improving the economics of the wider process.

A practical approach to forecasting and measuring enterprise AI ROI

Given the difficulty of establishing the costs and financial value of AI with confidence, the figures used in an ROI estimate need to be well grounded, and any assumptions used to derive them should be explicit and open to testing.

The following considerations can help enterprises build and test more credible estimates.

Translate AI-driven process improvements into financial value

Enterprises can use a pre-AI baseline to measure how process outcomes change after AI is introduced. However, a simple before-and-after comparison may be misleading if other conditions change at the same time. For example, sales might rise after an AI tool is introduced simply because demand happened to increase at the same time. A/B tests, staggered rollouts, or comparisons between similar teams using and not using AI can help tease out how much of the change is due to AI rather than those other effects.

Once an improvement can be attributed to AI, enterprises can quantify its financial value. This can be relatively straightforward when the financial effect of the improvement can be measured directly — like if AI increases conversion rates and the additional sales generate $200,000 in gross profit.

Other improvements are harder to value because their financial effects are further downstream. For example, an AI-enabled manufacturing process might lower the defect rate, which in turn lowers rework, returns, or warranty costs. In cases like this, enterprises need to estimate the financial value of the AI-driven improvement from the resulting cost savings.

Establish the full cost of delivering AI in production

Model and inference costs are among the most visible costs of running AI, but they represent only part of the total cost. A credible ROI estimate also includes upfront implementation costs and ongoing technical and operational costs, such as infrastructure, integrations, monitoring, human oversight, and engineering support.

Model and inference costs are among the most visible costs of running AI, but they represent only part of the total cost.

Some of those costs are easy to miss because they sit inside existing technology or operating budgets rather than appearing as separate AI expenses. For example, if engineers spend part of their time maintaining AI-related integrations, or if AI workloads consume centrally funded infrastructure capacity, the ROI calculation should reflect the cost of the resources AI actually uses.

Stress-test ROI at production scale and over an appropriate time horizon

Enterprises can sharpen their ROI forecasts by testing them against several plausible production scenarios. For example, they can vary assumptions about expected usage volume, workload mix, production costs, and financial value to see which factors matter most and how far they can change before the business case breaks down. Once AI is in production, enterprises can use actual usage, cost, and financial data to update those forecasts.

The forecast’s time horizon matters too. AI investments can incur significant upfront costs before their full benefits are realized, so a short forecast period can understate AI’s longer-term returns. But longer-range forecasts also become less reliable given the unpredictability of future changes to AI costs, capabilities, and business conditions. Enterprises can manage that tradeoff by modeling ROI over several future time horizons to see when the investment is expected to break even and how much of the projected return depends on longer-term assumptions.

Final thoughts

ROI analysis helps enterprises decide where to scale, redesign, or pull back AI use as model capabilities improve and costs change. As teams gain experience with AI, they may also develop entirely new AI-enabled products, services, or ways of working that weren’t part of the original business case. Enterprises can then assess the value created by these innovations relative to what the business would likely have achieved without them.

item.title: [Hugging Face] Granite Switch 4.1: Chat, Decisions, and Speech from One End…
item.description: Full title: Granite Switch 4.1: Chat, Decisions, and Speech from One Endpoint
item.content:encoded:
Back to Articles

Granite Switch 4.1: Chat, Decisions, and Speech from One Endpoint

Enterprise Article

Published October 15, 2026

8

Kate Soule

katesoule

ibm-granite

Subhajit Chaudhury

subhajit1412

ibm-granite

Hendrik Strobelt

hen

ibm-granite

Luis A Lastras

GrizleeBer

ibm-granite

Introduced last spring, the Granite Switch project enables a modular approach to model development. Now Granite Switch 4.1 models, armed with a Decision adapter and the fastest ASR model on the OpenASR leaderboard, can move efficiently between natural-language responses, general and specialized decisions, and speech-to-text tasks—all from one hosted endpoint.

Specifically, Granite-Switch-4.1-8B and -30B models are configured to include:

  • A new Decision aLoRA for general-purpose decision-making (e.g. v1/systemone),
  • A specialized Guardian aLoRA that, on average, outperforms Jev 1.13, Microsoft-Decision-1, GPT-Luna-Decisions, and Clef-Flash on safety-related decision tasks, and
  • Granite-Speech-5.0-Turbo-CTC, the fastest ASR model on the OpenASR Leaderboard, embedded for use in transcription tasks.

All three of these technologies (along with the underlying base model) are composed into one model, taking up approximately the same amount of VRAM on a GPU as the base model would by itself. That means more capabilities with fewer GPUs.

And because the Switch adapters were built as cache-efficient Activated LoRAs, the KV cache created from a base model generation can be reused for any subsequent adapter-based decisions. Combined with our team's recent vLLM contributions to speed up low rank adapter inferencing, as well as a co-located ASR encoder, Granite Switch 4.1 models can switch between a chat request and a decision request and a spoken request, with blazing fast speeds.

Check out our Speech-to-Decisions HF space where granite-switch-4.1-8b transcribes audio, generates summaries, screens for harmful content, and tests 15 other user-defined flags—all running on a single endpoint in real time.

Granite Libraries: The OG Decision Models

Decision models aren’t new. Our previous release of Granite Libraries features a repository of specialized “decision model” adapters and other specialized task adapters that can be composed into custom Granite Switch models. And while Jev and other closed decision models focus on generality, we’ve found that many of our specialized granitelib adapters can outperform generalists on specialized classification tasks.

Compare granitelib adapters with generalist decision models when evaluated on specialized classification tasks.

Because adapters share the base model's KV cache, adding specialists alongside a generalist decision adapter costs almost nothing. You get broad coverage from the generalist and higher accuracy from specialists on the tasks you care about.

In a “Race” between Granite-Switch-4.1-30B (frozen base Granite + 4 specialized aLoRAs) and Jev-27B (frozen base Qwen model + 1 generic decision LoRA), Granite-Switch-4.1-30B was able to complete a real world, 5-step RAG workflow much faster than its competitor.

Compose and Extend Your Own Granite Switch Model

Granite-Switch-4.1-8B and -30B are released with “batteries included”. They are Granite Switch models that we compiled with a predefined set of helpful adapters. But you don’t need to use our version. Anyone can compose their own Granite Switch model, mixing and matching adapters from Granite Libraries to best meet their needs.

Moving forward, we see tremendous opportunity for the community to compose and extend Granite Switch models with custom and third party adapters. We plan to release an Adapter SDK for training adapters in Mellea, along side other tutorials and Granite Switch support. These adapters could be specialized classification adapters to augment decision-based workflows or adapters for specialized language tasks. You could even use custom adapters to teach a 3B parameter version of Granite to play the classic game Doom.

Similarly to Jev, our custom 3B parameter Granite Switch model made split second decisions to navigate the Doom game, but was able to do so at 60 - 100 decisions / second, compared to Jev’s reported 10 decisions / second.1 Unlike Jev, this Granite Switch model can also narrate and respond to your questions while it is playing.

We look forward to releasing more details and data on Granite Switch in the upcoming weeks, but until then, we encourage you to try out our latest Switch models and these other helpful resources for getting started.

Resources for Getting Started

  • Granite Switch 4.1 Model Cards
  • Speech-to-Decisions Demo
  • Granite Switch GitHub Repo
  • Original Granite Switch and Granite Libraries Release Blog
  • Create your own aLoRA v LoRA race on Colab.

Footnotes

1 https://typesafe.ai/blog/introducing-system-one-models-and-jev

item.title: [Hugging Face] Apertus 1.5 Release Notes
item.content:encoded:
Back to Articles

Apertus 1.5 Release Notes

Team Article

Published October 15, 2026

36

Hanna Yukhymenko

hannayukhymenko

swiss-ai

Oleg Lavrovsky

loleg

swiss-ai

Y Metz

ymetz

swiss-ai

Our latest release, Apertus 1.5, extends the 8B and 70B Apertus 1.0 models with image/audio understanding, an optional thinking mode, a four times longer context window, improved instruction-following, and better tool use. The updated 8B and 70B model weights were released to Hugging Face on July 24, 2026 under an Apache 2.0 license. Further details are now available from the project Technical Report, and summarized here.

Apertus 1.5 is a continued pretraining of the first generation model: adding 4 trillion tokens of text and multimodal training data to the 8B model and 2 trillion tokens to the 70B model, for a total of 19T and 17T, respectively. As with every Apertus release, the models are fully open: open weights, open data, open values, and full training details.

Key Enhancements

  • Native Multimodal Understanding: Apertus 1.5 accepts images and audio alongside text, bringing documents, diagrams, and photos into the conversation. The models can also process spoken language, though this remains experimental.
  • Thinking Mode: The models can be switched into a thinking mode to reason about the input before answering, which improves performance on reasoning problems.
  • Long Context: The context window grows to 262,144 tokens, a 4x increase over Apertus 1.0.
  • Improved Instruction-Following: Better instruction adherence than Apertus 1.0 gives more predictable and accurate responses.
  • Improved Tool Use: The models are trained for better tool integration, allowing more effective use of external tools and APIs.
  • Open Values: Stronger adherence to the Apertus Charter, which brings transparency to the model’s values and principles.

Training Process

The full Apertus 1.5 training pipeline

Multimodality Through the Tokenizer

We introduce multimodality in v1.5 models in an early-fusion manner, where images and audio enter Apertus as discrete tokens in the same sequence with text tokens, instead of using a separate vision encoder. Images are tokenized with the Emu3.5 tokenizer (a 512×512 image becomes 1,024 tokens) and audio with WavTokenizer (40 tokens per second). We only extend the vocabulary, so the architecture stays unchanged and training runs at text-only speed. The models understand images and audio but generate only text.

Pre-Training

Starting from Apertus 1.0, we continue pretraining in four stages:

  • Unpaired: text plus standalone images and audio, so the model learns the new modalities.
  • Paired: image–caption and audio–transcript pairs, so it aligns them with language.
  • Cooldown: higher-quality data with more math and code.
  • Long context: the window grows step by step from 8k to 262k tokens.

Overall, more than half of the training tokens are text-only, which preserves the language abilities of Apertus 1.0. The text data is refreshed with sources such as FineWeb2-HQ+, FinePDFs, and Nemotron-CC. All new data, multimodal included, meets the same bar as before: publicly available, permissively licensed, and with robots.txt opt-outs respected retroactively. Every source is listed in apertus-data-transparency.

Post-Training

Post-training runs in five stages: SFT → long-context SFT → RL → DPO → charter alignment (SDPO).

  • SFT on 3.7M text samples plus image and speech data. Reasoning traces are added only to prompts the model can't already solve without them. Tool-use data is restricted to execution-verified trajectories. We release the text SFT mix we used on Hugging Face.
  • Long-context SFT at the full 262k window restores the long-context ability that short-context SFT erodes.
  • RL with verifiable rewards (RLVR) on about 350k math, code, instruction-following, multilingual, and vision prompts, mixing thinking on and off.
  • DPO with judge-scored preference pairs improves chat quality, tool use, and safety. We release the preference pool and training pairs.
  • SDPO aligns the model with the Apertus Charter through judge feedback and self-distillation.

Evaluation Results

Alongside the extended model capabilities, we also significantly expanded the scope of evaluations. Beyond the existing text-based evaluations used for Apertus 1.0, we added multimodal evaluations (image & audio), and thinking-mode evaluations.

The multimodal evaluations are done through MLLM-eval-suite pipeline, merging two major multimodal evaluation frameworks lmms-eval and VLMEvalKit. We also added a series of text-based benchmarks, as well as extended benchmarking for translation and multilingual capabilities, safety, and tool use. These can be found in our post-training evaluation repository, based on lm-evaluation-harness fork.

While still trailing frontier open-weight models, the new release has also significantly improved performance in coding and instruction following capabilities with Apertus 1.5 8B outperforming similarly sized open-weight models on IF and multilingual tasks. Thinking further improves performance on challenging reasoning-heavy benchmarks like AIME. The multimodal performance of the model is closer to Gemma 4 12B and other current open-weight models. Apertus 1.5 multimodal performance is competitive in spatial understanding among open-weight models and document/chart understanding among open-source models.

We also thank our collaborators and external evaluators for their help with efficient benchmarking of Apertus capabilities. In particular, Apertus 1.5 shows strong performance on Swiss Legal tasks, being on par with leading open-weight models (blog, code). Additionally, on Last Translation Benchmark, Apertus 1.5 8B presents machine translation capabilities which match GPT-OSS-20B and outperform models like Claude Haiku 4.5 or Google Translate (leaderboard, paper).

Evaluation Cards: Apertus ❤️ EvalEval

Apertus collaborates with the EvalEval Coalition to ensure fully transparent and reproducible benchmarking. We publish the Apertus 1.5 results in the Every Eval Ever (EEE) schema, a shared format that records not only scores, but also who ran the evaluation, how the model was accessed, the generation settings, and how each metric should be interpreted: details that are routinely missing from leaderboards and that often explain why similar-looking scores differ.

The results are shown in the Eval Card below, which combines the run data with benchmark and model metadata into one interpretable record, and are also available through Hugging Face Community Evals. This is the same infrastructure the UK AI Security Institute uses to publish its evaluations openly. Since our text evaluations run on our public fork of lm-evaluation-harness, which EEE supports with a dedicated converter, anyone can rerun them and compare their numbers against ours under identical settings.

Structured evaluation reporting also matters beyond research. EvalEval has mapped Evaluation Cards to AI governance requirements, including Article 55 of the EU AI Act and the GPAI Code of Practice, and found that the EEE schema can represent 56 of the 60 evaluation-reporting elements these frameworks call for. This fits how we already release Apertus: alongside the models, we publish a Public Summary of Training Content and, voluntarily, a Code of Practice document. Machine-readable evaluation records are a natural next step: making it easier for regulators, deployers, and researchers to find, interpret, and compare the evidence behind a model.

We are committed to promoting reproducible and transparent evaluation through Eval Cards and the EEE schema, and encourage other model developers to report their results in the same way, so that scores can be compared across models and organizations.

Apertus 1.5 Reproducibility

All recipes, ablations, and data mixtures are documented in the Technical Report. We aim to popularize open model development by making the v1.5 training process public and accessible. Intermediate checkpoints are hosted in our Apertus 1.5 Hugging Face collection, including the base weights, SFT, RLVR and DPO, as well as our curated training data mixes/custom datasets in Apertus 1.5 datasets collection. Sharing them allows researchers to investigate how each stage changes the model behavior.

The report covers numerous ablations on the effect of post-training data in different stages, where we observed that the multimodal data mixed in together with text data during SFT helps improve across all modalities. We also find that the benefits of multimodal reasoning traces survive the subsequent text-only reinforcement learning: starting from an SFT checkpoint trained with multimodal traces, RL improves mathematics more than when starting from a text-only checkpoint, and the advantage on reasoning tasks persists throughout training.

Models8B70B

Model Availability

Proton Lumo and Infomaniak Euria are two widely used apps that have recently integrated Apertus 1.5. These deployments are linked in the Community Showcase among others - see this discussion thread for a preview.

Access to Apertus 1.5 in the form of an API for developers has been announced by a range of providers, including Swisscom, Infomaniak, Phoeniqs, and other companies listed in our General Availability guide. The report also provides details on how we work with external evaluators to test and prepare the models.

Technical instructions for running the models are in the model cards of the Apertus releases on Hugging Face and in our Quickstart guide.

How to Get Involved

Thank you for reading this blog post and being part of our community! We just celebrated five million downloads in our Hugging Face analytics 🤗 and are not slowing down. At the recent AI+X Summit in Zurich, our team announced the roadmap for Apertus 2.0: sparse/MoE architecture, ~600B total parameters, extended training schedule, with agents, mathematics and coding as priorities.

In summary: we invite you to read our report, download the models, explore the intermediate checkpoints, finetune the weights, and reproduce our evaluations. Questions that are not already covered in our publications or website FAQ are always welcome, and we would also love to hear which topics would be most useful to the community for future deep dives.

If you build with or use Apertus, please fill out the Showcase form, and reach out through the options on our Contact page. We are looking forward to highlighting more work, learning what you are building, and hearing how Apertus can be improved!

Citation

Welcome Muse Spark Open: open-weight frontier multimodal mixture-of-experts model from Meta

Published October 15, 2026

Update on GitHub

24

Pedro Cuenca

pcuenq
