item.title: [AI21 Labs] AI21 Partners with Gong, Deel and Alice to Post-Train Specia…
item.description: Full title: AI21 Partners with Gong, Deel and Alice to Post-Train Specialized Models on NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL
item.content:encoded:
Over the past three weeks, our team of Forward-Deployed Researchers (FDRs) post-trained recently released NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL in partnership with Gong, Deel, and Alice to deliver specialized models that surpass or match frontier quality on their defined use case – yet at a fraction of the cost.

As companies increasingly seek to own specialized intelligence, rather than rent general models, AI21’s Lab-as-a-Service offering and proprietary Harness and Model training platform allow companies to make that transition in weeks, not quarters.

The motivation to stop renting, and start owning, intelligence, varies across companies. For some, it’s cost; for others, it’s control over their data or their differential edge. As training partners, our FDRs carefully build post-training recipes and custom evaluations to support customer objectives.

This post dives into the business impact and differentiation enabled by post-training sovereign specialized intelligence, and the methods our FDRs used to get there.

An open foundation for specialized intelligence

NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL is an open multimodal model for long-running agents that need to see, reason and act. Engineered for high-accuracy agentic execution, it is designed to be post-trained on an organization’s own data, tools and policies.

Specialized model #1: Matching frontier quality on Gong’s Data Extractor at a fraction of the cost

Post-training objective: Reduce cost without harming quality

Use case summary

Leading revenue AI company Gong developed an agent, Gong Data Extractor, that reviews customer interactions – such as calls, emails, and web conferences – to identify the key deal and account information vital to revenue teams. It stores these as fields which are automatically updated as new information comes in and can be synced to customer CRM records: everything from deal stage to health scores.

Frontier models summarize deals well. Yet at the scale Gong is working at, processing tens of millions of interactions a month, cost compounds quickly. So far, no cheaper model has been able to match frontier quality on this use case – and sacrificing quality on customer records was non-negotiable.

Methods

The AI21 FDR team collaborated with Gong to post-train Nemotron 3.5 Super to match the quality demanded by such a high-stakes use case, but with all the cost benefits of an efficient, open model. Within just two weeks, the teams built out a unique training dataset, implemented a mixture of SFT and DPO training techniques, and built out the necessary evaluation infrastructure to gate quality on the CRM edits, with extra evaluation layers applied to high-risk metrics.

Results

After post-training NVIDIA’s Nemotron 3.5 Super, Gong’s own evaluations found that the specialized model matches SOTA models like Claude Opus 5.5 in terms of speed and accuracy, and at a small fraction of the cost.

Specialized model #2: Raising accuracy on Deel’s Payroll QA Model to 8% higher than the frontier, while costing 33x less

Post-training objective: Cementing a proprietary edge that frontier models can’t beat

Use case summary

Deel, the global HR and payroll platform, supports more than 40,000 companies across 150+ countries, answering payroll questions that span multiple countries and jurisdictions. What constitutes the right answer depends on local tax rules, employment contracts and company policies – and all three change regularly. Frontier models know most of these rules individually, yet often leaves part of the answer out. In payroll, though, a partial answer is a wrong answer. Deel wanted an open model that gives the complete answer unprompted, at a fraction of frontier cost.

Methods

For this effort, the AI21 FDR team relied on expert-verified training data and benchmarks from Emet by Deel, a frontier AI evaluation lab that builds benchmarks and expert-generated training data. Building on that foundation, the AI21 FDR team first determined through initial testing that Nemotron 3.5 Super has the required knowledge to answer most of the questions, and could benefit from adapting the model’s behavior to match the level of detail and style expected. In order to bake the desired behavior into the model weights, the FDR team followed a two-step training recipe, beginning with SFT on pruned generated rollouts, followed by SDPO (self distillation policy optimization) in which the teacher gained hindsight by conditioning on detailed instructions on the desired behavior.

Results

As a result of AI21’s post-training efforts on Nemotron 3.5 Super VL, answer accuracy rose to 72% on Emet’s 8-country payroll benchmark evaluation, sitting 8 points above Claude Opus 5.5, and costing 33x less per query.

Specialized model #3: Training Nemotron 3.5 Super with Alice’s RL environments to improve attack resilience by 41 points

Post-training objective: Preserving strict control over enterprise data

Use case summary

Alice, an AI safety and security company, builds RL gyms, where customers can train production agents to combat security threats to the real software platforms where they work. RL Environments customers benefit from Alice’s “Rabbit Hole” dataset – sourced from real-world intel on threat actor behavior, as well as input from 150+ staff security researchers and expert network members – and now a post-trained model that is primed to detect indirect prompt injection attacks in both Slack and Github.

Methods

Working closely alongside Alice, our FDR team started by evaluating Nemotron 3.5 Super on their RL gym. In order to improve initial results of the model and increase diversity amongst its answers, the FDR team first applied SFT and DPO training methods. Afterwards, once the trained model had good enough initial performance and diversity, the team brought in GRPO (Online RL) training to further increase the results

Results

Together, AI21 and Alice improved Nemotron 3.5 Super’s attack resilience by 41 points without harming overall task performance, outperforming frontier models like GPT-6.1 Sol. Read more about the collaboration in Alice’s [blog].

Paving the way to AI independence

The three tasks described above cover a wide range of enterprise work, from summarization to knowledge-intensive retrieval to attack resilience. What these tasks do have in common is a repetitive load of up to millions of queries a month and exacting standards of what ‘right’ looks and sounds like, that frontier models can’t always capture.

Post-training Nemotron 3.5 Super on our Harness and Model training platform – directed by our team of FDRs – took all three tasks from the baseline evaluated to specialized intelligence in three weeks, reducing cost and establishing an edge competitors can’t rent and full control over agent behavior.

If you are ready to move forward on the path to AI independence, get in touch.

item.title: [Anyscale] Running Ray at scale on Kubernetes with KubeRay
item.content:encoded:
HomeBlogBlog Detail

Running Ray at scale on Kubernetes with KubeRay

By Nai-Jui Yeh, Chun-Hao Wan and Philip Wang | October 15, 2026

LinkWhat is KubeRay

Ray is an open-source framework for scaling Python and AI workloads across many machines. It handles everything from distributed training to online serving through a single Python API, so users can write code once and run it on a laptop or a thousand-node cluster.

Kubernetes, on the other hand, is where most organizations already run their infrastructure. GPUs, quotas, access control, networking, and monitoring are all managed there. Teams that adopt Ray rarely want a second cluster manager alongside Kubernetes. They want Ray to run on the Kubernetes they already have.

The challenge is that Kubernetes only understands its own native resources like Pods, Services, and Jobs. It has no concept of a Ray cluster, a Ray job, or a Ray Serve application. Running Ray directly on Kubernetes therefore means writing your own glue: Deployments for the head and workers, a Service for the head, scripts to submit jobs and wait for them, and custom logic to scale workers or recover from failures. Every team ends up rebuilding the same plumbing.

KubeRay closes this gap. It is an open-source Kubernetes operator that brings Ray into the Kubernetes ecosystem, providing Kubernetes-native lifecycle management, autoscaling, scheduling, reliability, and observability for Ray workloads. KubeRay is the standard way to run Ray on Kubernetes today, and is the foundation of the managed Ray offerings from major cloud providers.

KubeRay introduces three custom resources: RayCluster for a long-running Ray cluster, RayJob for a single job with its own ephemeral cluster, and RayService for Ray Serve applications. We describe how these resources work in the Architecture section below.

LinkBefore and after KubeRay

While generic Kubernetes may initially handle the infrastructure Ray needs to run on, it struggles to understand Ray itself including, so every platform team ends up hand-writing the same deployments, services, submission scripts, and recovery logic to fill that missing gap. KubeRay replaces that manual work with a Kubernetes-native resource for each of the following tasks.

TaskGeneric KubernetesKubeRay
Start a Ray clusterHand-write Deployments for the head and workers and a Service for the head, and keep them in sync yourselfDefine a RayCluster. The operator creates and manages the head Pod, head Service, and worker Pods
Run a batch jobWrite scripts to submit the job, poll for completion, and tear down the cluster afterwardDefine a RayJob. KubeRay creates a dedicated RayCluster, submits the job, and cleans it up when the job finishes
Serve a modelHand-roll a Deployment and Service for Ray Serve, plus your own health checks and rollout logicDefine a RayService. KubeRay keeps Serve applications available through cluster and head-node failures and supports zero-downtime upgrades
Scale with demandRely on the Kubernetes Horizontal Pod Autoscaler, which has no visibility into Ray tasks, actors, or placement groupsRay-aware autoscaling that scales worker groups based on pending tasks, actors, and placement groups
Recover from a head-node failureWrite custom logic to detect the failure and rebuild cluster stateGlobal Control Service (GCS) fault tolerance recovers cluster metadata automatically while keeping Ray Serve applications running
Monitor and operateBuild your own tooling to surface Ray-specific statusKubernetes-native status and Events, plus kubectl ray for a familiar CLI experience

LinkWhere KubeRay fits between Ray and Kubernetes

Where KubeRay fits between Ray and Kubernetes

KubeRay sits between Kubernetes and Ray, and it does not replace either scheduler. Kubernetes schedules Pods onto nodes while Ray schedules tasks and actors onto the CPUs and GPUs inside those Pods. KubeRay bridges the two: it turns a RayCluster spec into Pods, and reports Ray's state back to Kubernetes as status fields and events.

This layering also splits responsibilities cleanly between two roles. Platform teams work at the Kubernetes and operator layers: they install KubeRay once, then manage node pools, quotas, access control, and monitoring with the tools they already use. Ray users, such as ML engineers and data scientists, work at the Ray and application layers: they write Ray code and execute the code on top of the custom resource (RayCluster, RayJob or RayService) KubeRay creates.

LinkWhat KubeRay provides

KubeRay Operator

KubeRay is a Kubernetes operator with one controller per custom resource. RayCluster is the building block: the operator turns it into a head Pod, a head Service, and worker Pods. RayJob and RayService each own a RayCluster and add what their workload needs: a submitter for RayJob, and Serve applications plus a Serve Service for RayService.

LinkKey features

LinkRayCluster

  • Ray-aware autoscaling. Automatically scale worker groups based on workload demand, including pending tasks, actors, and placement groups.
  • Global Control Service (GCS) fault tolerance. Recover Ray cluster metadata after a head-node failure while keeping Ray Serve applications running.
  • Heterogeneous compute. Run worker groups with different CPU and accelerator configurations in the same RayCluster.

LinkRayJob

  • Ephemeral clusters: Create a dedicated RayCluster for each job and clean it up when the job finishes.
  • Multiple submission modes: Submit jobs through Kubernetes Jobs, HTTP, sidecars, or interactive mode.
  • Lifecycle management: Configure retries, deadlines, and cleanup policies based on job outcomes.

LinkRayService

  • Kubernetes-native Ray Serve: Define and manage Ray Serve applications as part of your Kubernetes workload.
  • High availability: Keep Ray Serve applications available through cluster and head-node failures.
  • Zero-downtime upgrades: Upgrade Ray applications and clusters without interrupting serving traffic, with support for blue-green and incremental upgrades.

LinkKubernetes Scheduling

  • Kueue and MultiKueue: Integrate Ray workloads with Kubernetes resource quotas and multi-cluster scheduling.
  • Gang scheduling: Support gang scheduling with Kubernetes Workload API, Volcano, YuniKorn, scheduler-plugins, and NVIDIA KAI Scheduler.
  • Resource and label-aware scheduling: Expose Kubernetes resources and labels to Ray for resource- and label-based scheduling.

LinkSecurity

  • Ray token authentication: Secure Ray clusters with token-based authentication.
  • Kubernetes RBAC authentication: Use existing Kubernetes RBAC policies to control access to Ray clusters.
  • mTLS and NetworkPolicy: Encrypt Ray Pod-to-Pod traffic and isolate Ray clusters with Kubernetes NetworkPolicies.

LinkObservability

  • Metrics and dashboards: Monitor Ray workloads and KubeRay with Prometheus and Grafana.
  • Kubernetes-native status and events: Track workload lifecycle and troubleshoot Ray resources through Kubernetes status and Events.
  • History Server: Preserve Ray events and logs in object storage and inspect them after a cluster has been deleted.

LinkTooling

  • kubectl ray: Simplify managing Ray clusters on Kubernetes with a familiar command-line experience.
  • KubeRay API Server: Provide simplified APIs for platforms and user interfaces to manage KubeRay resources.

LinkHow to deploy KubeRay

KubeRay works with any Kubernetes cluster. Get started by installing the KubeRay operator, then create a Ray workload using Kubernetes-native resources.

1. Install KubeRay

Follow the Getting Started with KubeRay guide to install the operator onto your Kubernetes cluster. KubeRay has been tested on managed Kubernetes services including Amazon EKS, Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE), and Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS).

2. Choose your workload

KubeRay provides these custom resources for running Ray workloads:

  • RayCluster: Run a Ray cluster for development and prototyping.
  • RayJob: Run batch workloads with a dedicated RayCluster, with automatic cluster creation and cleanup.
  • RayService: Deploy and manage Ray Serve applications with high availability and zero-downtime upgrades.
  • RayCronJob: Run RayJobs on a recurring schedule using a cron expression.

3. Deploy with Kubernetes

Deploying a Ray workload with KubeRay is as simple as applying a Kubernetes custom resource.

For example, a RayJob runs a batch training workload and manages the Ray cluster used by the job. KubeRay creates the RayCluster, waits for it to become ready, submits the training job, and can clean up the cluster when the job finishes.

Here's an example of training a PyTorch model on the Fashion MNIST dataset with CPUs on Kubernetes, showing KubeRay creating the RayCluster, running the training workload, tracking its completion, and managing the cluster lifecycle.

The training code uses Ray Train, while KubeRay uses a RayJob to run and manage it on Kubernetes.

kubectl apply -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ray-project/kuberay/v1.7.0/ray-operator/config/samples/pytorch-mnist/ray-job.pytorch-mnist.yaml

After applying the RayJob, KubeRay creates the RayCluster and its Pods. Check the RayJob and verify that the RayCluster Pods are running:

kubectl get rayjob
NAME                   JOB STATUS   DEPLOYMENT STATUS   RAY CLUSTER NAME             START TIME             END TIME   AGE
rayjob-pytorch-mnist   PENDING      Running             rayjob-pytorch-mnist-9s4p2   2026-09-30T02:40:15Z              37s

kubectl get pod
NAME                                                  READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
kuberay-operator-799d594664-h5czx                     1/1     Running   0          19m
rayjob-pytorch-mnist-9s4p2-head-b6q6z                 1/1     Running   0          39s
rayjob-pytorch-mnist-9s4p2-small-group-worker-k6786   1/1     Running   0          39s
rayjob-pytorch-mnist-9s4p2-small-group-worker-thhgx   1/1     Running   0          39s
rayjob-pytorch-mnist-v4dvt                            1/1     Running   0          11s

The RayJob then submits the training workload to the newly created RayCluster. After the training finishes, the RayJob reaches SUCCEEDED:

kubectl get rayjob
NAME                   JOB STATUS   DEPLOYMENT STATUS   RAY CLUSTER NAME             START TIME             END TIME               AGE
rayjob-pytorch-mnist   SUCCEEDED    Complete            rayjob-pytorch-mnist-9s4p2   2026-09-30T02:40:15Z   2026-09-30T02:48:33Z   8m47s

You can inspect the training results from the submitter Pod:

kubectl logs rayjob-pytorch-mnist-v4dvt

2026-09-29 19:40:48,610 INFO cli.py:41 -- Job submission server address: http://rayjob-pytorch-mnist-9s4p2-head-svc.default.svc.cluster.local:8265
2026-09-29 19:40:49,584 SUCC cli.py:65 -- -------------------------------------------------------
2026-09-29 19:40:49,584 SUCC cli.py:66 -- Job 'rayjob-pytorch-mnist-5s4p4' submitted successfully
2026-09-29 19:40:49,584 SUCC cli.py:67 -- -------------------------------------------------------
...
(RayTrainWorker pid=975, ip=10.244.0.12) 
Train Epoch 0:  77%|███████▋  | 1436/1875 [00:15<00:04, 91.08it/s] [repeated 92x across cluster]
(RayTrainWorker pid=975, ip=10.244.0.12) 
Train Epoch 0:  92%|█████████▏| 1719/1875 [00:18<00:01, 88.59it/s]
...
(RayTrainWorker pid=975, ip=10.244.0.12) Reporting training result 10: TrainingReport(checkpoint=None, metrics={'loss': 0.3702628721599095, 'accuracy': 0.8646}, validation_spec=None)
2026-09-29 19:48:30,801 SUCC cli.py:65 -- ------------------------------------------
2026-09-29 19:48:30,801 SUCC cli.py:66 -- Job 'rayjob-pytorch-mnist-5s4p4' succeeded
2026-09-29 19:48:30,801 SUCC cli.py:67 -- ------------------------------------------

For more ready-to-use examples, see the KubeRay sample configurations for RayCluster, RayJob, RayService, and RayCronJob. Enjoy running Ray on Kubernetes with KubeRay!

LinkJoin the Ray community

KubeRay is built in the open. Connect with the community, share feedback, and contribute:

  • Ask questions in the #kuberay channel on the Ray Slack workspace.
  • Meet the community at the bi-weekly KubeRay community meeting. You can find the schedule on the Ray/KubeRay LFX calendar.
  • Help shape the roadmap by sharing your feature requests and feedback on kuberay#2999.

Table of contents

  • What is KubeRay
  • Before and after KubeRay
  • Where KubeRay fits between Ray and Kubernetes
  • What KubeRay provides
  • Key features
  • How to deploy KubeRay
  • Join the Ray community

item.title: [Anthropic Claude] Agent observability on the Claude Platform
item.content:encoded:
You can now send OpenTelemetry (OTel) traces from Claude Managed Agents, the Messages API, and Claude SDKs to any OTel tool, and follow each step your agents take. If you already send Claude Code or Cowork traces to your observability tool, the agents you build on the Claude Platform can also show up in the same place.

Trace agents with OpenTelemetry

Trusting an agent with more access starts with tracing its model calls, tool use, and MCP server calls. Review its traces, then widen its access as it proves reliable.

Add a destination in the Claude Console, and every agent turn, model call, and tool use arrives in your observability tool as a standard OpenTelemetry trace, with latency, tokens, and IDs.

Works with your observability tools

Claude traces follow the OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions, so data from Claude and other providers works in the same tools and dashboards.

  • Debug agents next to the rest of your stack. In Grafana Cloud, Honeycomb, Sentry, and Splunk, agent traces sit beside your logs and metrics, so you can see which service a slow or failed step came from.
  • Improve agents with production data. With Arize AI, Braintrust, Datadog, Langfuse, LangSmith by LangChain, New Relic, and PostHog, you can turn real traces into evals, catch quality issues, and measure whether a change helped.
  • Track usage across your organization. Send traces to Databricks Unity Gateway so platform and security teams can see token usage by team and flag unusual activity.

Claude traces also work with any other OpenTelemetry tool that accepts a standard OTLP endpoint.

Get started

OpenTelemetry traces on the Claude Platform is available in public beta. Managed Agents and the Messages API need a destination in the Claude Console, while Claude SDKs export traces automatically.

See the docs to get started.

Roman Shtylman, Co-Founder and CTO

item.title: [xAI Grok] Introducing Grok Voice 3.0
item.content:encoded:
Back to newsOct 14, 2026

Introducing Grok Voice 3.0

The world’s most intelligent voice model.

Try It FreeView Docs

Today, we’re announcing Grok Voice 3.0, the world’s most intelligent speech-to-speech model. It sets a new record for resolving customer support calls, has class-leading latency at under one second, and costs less than other frontier models. Grok Voice powers millions of conversations a day across Tesla and SpaceX, and is available today in the API at the same price as its predecessor.

The Most Accurate Voice Model

In Artificial Analysis’s independent testing, Grok Voice 3.0 ranks #1 on the Speech-to-Speech Index, with a score of 86.9. The Index combines speech reasoning, τ-Voice, and preference and task success from blind head-to-head calls. Grok Voice 3.0 also scores 97% on Full Duplex Bench, a measure of how naturally it handles pauses, turn-taking, and interruptions.

BenchmarkGrok Voice 3.0 (this release)Grok Voice 2.0GPT-Live-1(Astra, Medium)Gemini 3.8 Live(Ext. Thinking, High)
OverallAA Speech-to-Speech Index86.981.383.282.6
Speech ReasoningBig Bench Audio98.5%97.2%90.1%97.7%
Human PreferenceSpeech Agent Arena Elo107010111048990
Task CompletionTask Success Rate94.8%94.6%87.4%89.1%
Conversational DynamicsFull Duplex Bench97.0%95.1%94.9%91.9%

Source: Artificial Analysis, October 13, 2026.

τ-Voice measures how well agents handle support calls with diverse accents, background noise, and interruptions. Grok Voice 3.0 scores 71.6%, comparable with GPT-Live-1 (Astra), but at 40% lower latency, setting a new frontier in agent intelligence versus responsiveness.

Agentic Performance vs. Speed

τ-Voice

Source: Artificial Analysis

It's also cheaper to run than comparable models. Artificial Analysis measures what each model costs to complete a task in its Big Bench Audio run, and Grok Voice 3.0 comes in under both GPT-Live-1 (Astra, Medium) and GPT-Realtime-2.1.

Lower cost per task than comparable models

Average cost per task on Artificial Analysis's Big Bench Audio run, USD. Lower is better.

On EVA-Bench, ServiceNow’s benchmark for enterprise voice agents, Grok Voice 3.0 achieves the highest accuracy score at 74% and is the best-performing model when jointly scored across accuracy and customer experience.

“Grok Voice 3.0 sets a new Pareto frontier on EVA-Bench, ServiceNow’s open-source benchmark scoring voice agents on accuracy and experience across 200+ realistic enterprise scenarios. It pairs top accuracy with a natural, responsive conversation, setting a new standard for what enterprises can expect from AI on the front line of customer service.”

Nitin Aggarwal, Senior Director of Product Management, Agentic Evals and RAI, ServiceNow

Used by Millions of Customers at Tesla & SpaceX

Grok Voice 3.0 handles millions of conversations a day in Tesla vehicles. Drivers can use Connectors for simple requests like checking their calendar or answering an email, and Grok Bot for bigger tasks like ordering a coffee or booking dinner—all completely hands-free (see it on X). Grok Voice 3.0 also powers Grok Bot’s voice mode.

Starlink call centers use Grok Voice to answer 20,000 customer calls every day across multiple languages. Roughly 70% are resolved with no human in the loop, and one in four sales calls ends in a purchase before the caller hangs up. A single agent built on Grok Voice 3.0 verifies customers, troubleshoots hardware, issues credits, and ships replacement equipment.

Pricing and Availability

Grok Voice 3.0 is available today in the Voice Agent API at $0.08 / min ($4.80 / hr), the same price as Grok Voice 2.0. Agents using grok-voice-latest have already been switched over automatically, with no changes needed.

Start building with Grok Voice

Try It FreeView Docs

item.title: [Cohere] Lessons from scaling teams of coding agents: reach the front…
item.description: Full title: Lessons from scaling teams of coding agents: reach the frontier at 30% of the cost
item.content:encoded:
Oct 14, 2026

17 minute read

Lessons from scaling teams of coding agents: reach the frontier at 30% of the cost

Teams of coding agents are already building large-scale software, but how should they be organized to work most effectively and efficiently?

Key takeaways

  • Teams of agents unlock a new axis of inference-time scaling. On challenging coding tasks, well-organized teams outperform single agents, with gains of up to ~10 percentage points on ProgramBench. But these gains come at 3–7× higher cost. The question is not whether more agents help, but how to make that additional compute count.
  • Where you allocate agents matters more than how many you add. On ProgramBench, delegating only exploration and planning matches the performance of delegating planning, implementation, and verification together at half the cost. Collaboration pays off most when agents target the task's actual bottleneck.
  • A strong lead with cheap workers delivers near-frontier performance at 70% lower cost. A Sol lead coordinating 16 inexpensive Luna planning workers reaches 61.8% reward, compared with 63.2% for an all-Sol team delegating every stage, while reducing cost from $510 to $155.

Agent teams are building software

In the past year, teams of coding agents have moved from interesting demos to building large-scale software projects. Sixteen Claude agents wrote a 100,000-line C compiler that can build the Linux kernel, in a project that took about 2,000 agent sessions and $20,000 in API costs [1]. Cursor ran hundreds of agents that together wrote a web browser from scratch, more than a million lines of code, in about a week [2]. Bun was ported from Zig to Rust in 11 days, with 64 Claude agents running in parallel at its peak [3].

Each of these teams produced working software, but they differ from one another in many ways at once, from the models and roles to the scope of the projects themselves. The C compiler's agents worked as peers with no orchestrator and claimed tasks through lock files. Cursor used a hierarchical structure, with planners recursively decomposing work into subtasks delegated to hundreds of worker agents. Bun assigned fixed roles, giving each piece of work to one implementer, two adversarial reviewers, and one fixer.

Comparing them, however, says little about which design choices mattered or what they cost compared to a single agent. Factory's study of their own multi-agent system, which cycles an orchestrator, an implementer, and a validator in a fixed loop, shows how large that cost can be [4]. On one task, rebuilding the geospatial library GDAL, their three-role team more than doubled the reward achieved by a single agent, nearly reaching behavioral parity with the reference program, but cost 14 times as much and took 13 times as long.

So agent teams can do more than a single agent, but they cost more to run and usually take longer. This raises an important question: if a team of agents is a new way to spend inference compute, how should it be organized to be both effective and efficient? To answer it, we built a controlled testbed and ran teams of coding agents on it.

Figure 1. An illustrative run of a coding-agent team. A lead hands out work to its workers, who explore the original program, write code, and check it in a shared workspace.

A controlled testbed

A minimal harness

We built a deliberately minimal harness, inspired by mini-SWE-agent [5], so that we could change one design choice at a time. Every agent works through a simple bash tool, in one workspace shared by the whole team. One agent, the lead, receives the task and hands out work with a delegate_agent tool. A worker sees only the subtask it is given and reports back when it is done. Given the task, the lead dynamically decides how many workers to spawn, what each one does, and how to consolidate what they return.1

Each delegate_agent call either starts a new worker with a fresh context window or resumes a worker the lead has used before. A resumed worker keeps its prior context, so the lead can follow up with an agent that already knows part of the program. For example, the lead can ask a worker to fix the bugs in the code it wrote, instead of briefing a new worker from scratch.

From there, we vary five things:

  • Where the lead uses workers. We instruct the lead agent with two main prompts, which differ in how much guidance they give. The minimal prompt tells the lead that it is in charge of a team and asks it to give workers distinct, independent tasks, but leaves everything else, from how many workers to use to how to decompose the task, to the lead. The PIV prompt adds a structured workflow of exploring and planning (P), implementing (I), and verifying (V), and asks the lead to use workers in all three stages.
  • How the lead waits. A blocking lead waits for its workers to report back and does nothing in the meantime. An asynchronous lead keeps working while they run, and has two more tools, wait_for_updates to wait for the next report and list_agents to check on its workers.
  • Which models play which role. Does every agent on the team need the strongest, most expensive model? We test this with two kinds of teams. In a homogeneous team, the lead and its workers all run the same model. In a heterogeneous team, the lead keeps the strong model, but the workers run a cheaper one. Think of a senior engineer who directs the work and makes critical decisions, with junior engineers doing most of the legwork.
  • How many workers there are. Is a bigger team always better? To explore this, we compare two setups. In the first, the lead decides on its own how many workers it needs. In the second, we fix the team size at two, four, eight, or sixteen workers and see how reward and cost change as the team grows.
  • How agents communicate. By default, all communication goes through the lead, which hands out each subtask and receives each worker's report. In one set of runs, we provide agents with a send_message tool and let them message each other directly.

Figure 2. Two leads hand out the same subtasks, and each worker run takes the same time. The blocking lead sits idle until its workers report back. The asynchronous lead keeps working and starts the second round as soon as the first reports arrive. Bars are spans of work, downward arrows are calls to delegate_agent, and upward arrows carry reports back to the lead. Timings are illustrative.

ProgramBench

We test these choices on ProgramBench [6], a benchmark of 200 programs to rebuild from scratch. In each task, the agent starts from an empty workspace with the original program's executable, which it can run but not read, and that program's documentation. It has to probe the program to discover its interface, edge cases, and behavior, then write a new implementation that behaves the same way. We score each task by the share of a hidden suite of behavioral tests that the rebuilt program passes, and average this score over tasks to get the reward we report throughout.2

The tasks range from small command-line utilities like jq and ripgrep to large systems like SQLite, FFmpeg, and the PHP interpreter. The most challenging remain far out of reach. On FFmpeg, the best entry on the public leaderboard passes about 10% of tests.

Each task needs all three stages of the workflow, figuring out what the program does, writing it, and checking it against the original. That makes ProgramBench a good testbed for seeing which stages benefit from extra agents.

Figure 3. One ProgramBench task, dsq, a command-line tool that runs SQL queries over JSON, CSV, and other data files. The top panel is a solo Sol agent with the minimal prompt, and the bottom panel an asynchronous Sol team with the PIV prompt. The solo agent writes its program as one Python file, while the team splits it into modules, some written by workers. The team panel follows the files of one run, commands are simplified from the agents' own, and timings are illustrative.

We focus primarily on three GPT-5.6 models, Luna, Terra, and Sol, in increasing order of capability and cost. Unless noted otherwise, we ran each configuration three times on all 200 ProgramBench tasks and report averages over the three runs for reward, total cost, and total wall-clock time. A single task's score varied from run to run with a standard deviation of about 6 points, but the benchmark-wide average was far steadier, with a standard deviation of 0.5 points for a typical configuration and 1.4 for the noisiest. Every configuration ran on the same tasks, so we compare each team with its solo baseline task by task and report 95% confidence intervals of those differences.

We also ran Commit0-Lite [7], a set of 16 Python libraries whose implementations have been removed. The agent is given each library's repository skeleton, documentation, and unit tests, and has to fill in the code so that the tests pass. In ProgramBench, the agent has to work out what to build by running the original program. In Commit0, these provided materials spell it out, so the benchmark shows whether the same stages pay off when the specification is already given. With only 16 tasks, we use it as a secondary check.

Teams outperform solo agents, at a cost

We start with the simplest comparison, a single Sol agent against a team of Sol agents. With the same minimal prompt, a blocking team passed 61.8% of tests on average, against 52.1% for the solo agent. Giving the solo agent the PIV prompt closed part of that gap (57.7%), but a blocking team with the PIV prompt still came out about 5 points ahead (63.1%).

We also ran both prompts with an asynchronous lead, which can keep working while its workers run. All four Sol teams cost between 4 and 7 times as much as the corresponding solo agent. With the PIV prompt, the asynchronous team finished in 19.5% less time than the blocking one and reached about the same reward.

With the minimal prompt, the asynchronous team finished in 60% less time, but its lead did more of the work itself, delegating just 4.4 times per task, compared to 6.1 for the blocking lead. Its team gained only 3.8 points over the minimally prompted solo agent, against 9.7 for the blocking team, and at 55.9% it even fell below the PIV-prompted solo agent (57.7%).

Figure 4. Mean reward against inference cost (left) and wall-clock time (right), each the total for all 200 tasks averaged over three runs. Error bars are 95% intervals of each team's paired per-task difference from the corresponding solo agent.

Workers pay off most in planning

To find out where workers pay off, we instructed the lead to delegate subtasks to workers in just a single stage, while doing the other two stages itself. Under exploration and planning (P), workers run the program to learn its behavior and draft a plan, and the lead implements and verifies. Under implementation (I), workers write the code. Under verification (V), workers test the lead's implementation.

Planning was the clear winner. Among asynchronous teams, a lead that delegates only planning matched the reward of one that delegates every stage (63.6% against 63.2%) at half the cost ($249 against $510). Measured as reward gained per $100 of added cost, planning was about twice as efficient as the next-best stage.3

Figure 5. Asynchronous Sol teams that delegate one stage or all three. Means over three runs. Lines run from the solo PIV agent to each team. The dashed arrow runs from the PIV team to the planning team, which costs half as much. Error bars are paired 95% intervals relative to the solo PIV agent.

For example, on dsq, the solo agent with the PIV prompt passed 60% of its tests on average. Teams that delegate only planning passed 79% with an asynchronous lead and 76% with a blocking one, and each of their six runs beat every solo run. Teams that delegate implementation or verification passed only 58% to 71%.

The reason lies in the benchmark's design. The target program is a black box, so its behavior has to be discovered by running it. Planning workers do this in parallel, each probing a different part of the program's interface and handing the lead what it found. The lead then writes the code itself, with a much fuller picture of what to build.

Other works have reported related findings. Factory's validator begins by probing the reference program to build an executable standard of what "done" means, before any code is written [4]. Carlini's C-compiler team got unstuck on the Linux kernel by using GCC as an oracle to compare against [1]. In each case, knowing exactly what to build was the bottleneck, and putting compute there paid off.

Commit0 shows the other side of this. There, the repository already lays out what to build, and implementation, not planning, was the most effective stage to delegate in eight of our ten team setups. However, frontier models like GPT-5.6 Sol are close to saturating Commit0, with a capable solo agent already passing every test on 12 of the 16 tasks, which leaves only four tasks where the team could do better, so we treat this as suggestive rather than conclusive.

Planning workers can be cheap

If planning workers mostly gather information for the lead, do they need to be strong models? We kept Sol as the lead and swapped its planning workers for Luna, a much cheaper model. The team gave up a few points against the all-Sol team (60.5% against 63.6%). Measured against the solo agent, though, it kept 47.5% of the all-Sol team's gain for only 13.9% of its extra cost, so each dollar bought more than three times as much reward.

Now compare it with what we might have built without looking at the task. A natural comparison would have also been the PIV setup, where we tell a strong lead to use strong workers at every stage. That team reached 63.2%, but at a cost of $510. By recognizing that ProgramBench is bottlenecked on discovering what the program does, and putting cheap workers only on planning, we came within 2.7 points of it for a fifth of the cost.

Figure 6. The teams from Figure 5 together with two teams that pair a Sol lead with Luna workers (smaller worker dots), one delegating planning and one delegating all three stages. All teams are asynchronous. The dashed arrow runs from the all-Sol planning team to the Luna planning team, labeled with the Luna team's share of the all-Sol team's gain and extra cost, both measured from the solo PIV agent. Error bars are paired 95% intervals relative to the solo PIV agent.

To disentangle the lead's contribution from the workers', we held the workers fixed at Luna and upgraded the lead from Luna to Terra to Sol. Reward rose with every upgrade, from 42.5% to 51.6% to 60.5% (Figure 7), and each team beat a solo agent running its lead's model (37.4%, 47.2%, and 57.7%). Cheap workers could not make up for a weaker lead, though. A Terra lead with Luna workers still fell short of a Sol agent working alone (51.6% against 57.7%).

Figure 7. Mean reward against total inference cost (log scale) for solo PIV agents and asynchronous planning teams. Homogeneous teams, in which every agent uses the same model, have equal-sized dots, and heterogeneous teams, which pair a stronger lead with Luna workers, have smaller worker dots. The shaded band joins the three teams with Luna workers.

This matches recent work from Meta on meta-reasoning [8]. Their system splits an agent into a controller, which decides what to work on next and which earlier results to build on, and workers, which do that work. With the same workers and the same budget, a better controller scored higher on ProgramBench (71.5% against 63.7% with GPT-5.5), and its advantage grew as the budget increased while simpler control leveled off. In both their setup and ours, a stronger decision-maker raised what the same workers achieved.

Scaling the number of workers

So far, the lead chose how many workers to use. To see what more workers add, we fixed the team size, giving a Sol lead two, four, eight, or sixteen Luna workers. Planning teams improved the overall performance as they grew, from 59.6% with two to 61.8% with sixteen. Even at sixteen, Luna planners cost $155, 38% less than the all-Sol planning team ($249) and 70% less than the all-Sol team that delegates all three stages ($510), while staying within two points of both.

Implementation and verification workers behaved differently. They improved from two to four workers, then slipped slightly as more were added. Looking inside the runs shows why. Each planner ran the reference program about seven times, whatever the team size, so more planners showed the lead more of the program's behavior. Across the team, runs of the reference program grew from 15 with two planners to 109 with sixteen, and the planners' reports grew from 17,000 to 75,000 characters.

Extra implementers added no such information. Each one got a thinner slice of the plan, and assignments shrank from about 1,400 characters per worker with two implementers to 440 with sixteen. The implementers' share of the code grew from 54% with two to 85% with sixteen, but the lead checked the combined program against the reference no more often, at 5 to 6 runs whether it was combining two pieces or sixteen.

Figure 8. Reward of an asynchronous Sol lead with 2 to 16 Luna workers, by team size (left) and total cost (right). Each Luna-worker marker has one small dot per worker. Markers with equal-sized dots are all-Sol teams sized by the lead. Each fixed-size configuration is run once. Error bars are paired 95% intervals relative to the solo PIV agent.

Exploring communication

So far, agents only exchange information when the lead hands out work and when a worker reports back. We also tried giving every agent a send_message tool that can reach any other running agent.

In our runs, we noticed that the channel was used mostly to report upward. In Sol teams with the PIV prompt, 84% of messages went from workers to the lead, carrying interim findings, proposed interfaces, test failures, and questions.4 Messages between workers averaged fewer than one per task, and rose only to about one per task when workers were told to treat each other as collaborators.

Stronger models used the channel more. Sol agents wrote 3.4 to 5 times as much message text as Luna agents, and Sol leads sent more guidance back to their workers. Reward, however, stayed the same for Sol and Terra teams, and Luna teams lost 4 to 7 points. One possible explanation is that the stream of interim updates overwhelms a weaker lead, while a stronger one can absorb it. Another is that Luna workers used the tool poorly, with about half of their send_message calls malformed and rejected by the harness.

Figure 9. Asynchronous all-Luna, all-Terra, and all-Sol teams with a send_message tool. Hatched segments are rejected calls. Left: messages per task. Middle: amount of message text per task. Right: reward change against the same team without the tool, with paired 95% intervals.

That said, communication may still help in the right setting. Our harness is built around splitting up work and delegating it. Both the minimal and PIV prompts ask the lead to give workers distinct, independent tasks, so each worker has little that another worker needs. It makes sense, then, that workers messaged the lead far more than they messaged each other.

Contrasting this, Park et al. found that when agents share one goal and a common workspace, with no fixed roles, a team of five communicating agents matched the best of 33 independent agents on ARC-AGI-3 [9]. The key ingredient, which they call verified progress sharing, is that agents can check whether a teammate's discovery is actually an improvement. Agensh, a self-organizing harness from Microsoft, also reports cooperation emerging on its own in large flat teams [10].

How much agents talk to each other depends on the task, how the work is split, how agents are prompted, and how their models were trained. We would expect messaging to matter most when agents pursue the same goal, can check each other's progress, and are prompted to treat communication as part of the job, and we are actively exploring this in follow-up work.

How other models use a team

We also tested five other models with identical tools and prompts on a 30-task subset of ProgramBench (10 easy, 10 medium, and 10 hard tasks), and compared them with GPT-5.6 runs on those same tasks.5 For each model, we ran one trial for solo, blocking, and asynchronous teams using both the minimal and PIV prompt setups. With one run per model, differences of a few points may be noise.

The models used the team very differently. GPT-5.6 teams delegated often and gained up to 6.9 points over their best solo agent, and most of their team setups came out ahead. Claude Opus 4.8 behaved much the same, gaining 5.9 points with the PIV prompt and an asynchronous lead. Claude Opus 4.7 rarely delegated, at most 1.3 times per task, and its teams gained little over its best solo agent.6 Claude Haiku 4.5 and Gemini 3.7 Flash delegated as readily as GPT-5.6 but gained nothing from it. Gemini 3.8 Flash gained 3.1 points with the PIV prompt and a blocking lead, but lost 4.6 with an asynchronous one.

Figure 10. Delegations per task (left) and team lift over the best solo agent (right), on the 30-task subset of ProgramBench. For each model, lift is measured against whichever solo agent scored higher, with the minimal or the PIV prompt. Each marker is one of the four team setups. GPT-5.6 results average three runs on these 30 tasks. Other models are single runs, so differences smaller than about 5 points may be noise.

Two things have to go right for a team to help. The lead has to choose to delegate, and it has to make good use of what comes back. Opus 4.7 fell short on the first, and Haiku 4.5 and Gemini 3.7 Flash on the second. The two Opus models show how much this can change within one family. Opus 4.7 barely delegated, while the newer Opus 4.8 spread work across a team much as GPT-5.6 did, and gained from it. Whether newer models are generally better at leading a team is a question we cannot settle with one run per model.

The models also structured their programs differently. GPT-5.6 rebuilt most programs in Python (70% to 93% of submissions), whatever language the original was written in. Claude models reimplemented the program in its original language in 72% to 90% of submissions, and the Gemini Flash models fell in between (43% to 70%). Claude Opus 4.8 and both Gemini models also spread their programs over more files, a median of 5 to 11 source files per task against 1 to 3 for GPT-5.6.

What's next

Our results point to several directions we are excited about.

  • Hierarchy versus self-organization. On ProgramBench, a single lead can keep the whole program in view so a hierarchy works well. But a team of thousands of agents working over weeks would likely outgrow what any one lead can track. Such a team would have to decide who assigns roles, how information flows, and when to reorganize. At that scale, agents will need to share what they learn directly, perhaps through protocols they invent themselves. Pretraining already gives them the basic moves, such as reporting, asking, and delegating. Whether real coordination emerges from these as models scale, or has to be trained, is an open question that we see as central to scaling inference.
  • Alternative forms of communication. In our runs, messages mostly repeated what the lead would have received in reports anyway. Shared goals, shared progress logs, or messages that carry checkable evidence may give agents more reason to talk.
  • Adapting to the task. Planning paid off on ProgramBench because the specification has to be discovered, but on other tasks the bottleneck may be elsewhere. On Commit0, implementation helped most. A lead that can tell where its own task is stuck could move workers there without being told which stage to delegate.
  • Training models to lead. Models differed widely in how well they used a team, which suggests that leading is a skill that can be trained. A lead that delegates well, weighs conflicting reports, and knows when to wait could get more out of the same workers.

Much of what made our teams work depended on the lead: what it chose to delegate, and what it did with the reports that came back. As models get better at leading, the best way to organize a team may change too.

Footnotes

  • When the team size is dynamic, a lead can start at most five distinct workers per task, and beyond that it has to resume the ones it has. Raising the cap to twenty changed how the lead delegated but not how well the team did. The lead started more new workers instead of resuming old ones, the total number of delegations changed by at most 0.9 per task, and reward changed by between −1.6 and +1.6 points.
  • The ProgramBench authors rank models by the share of tasks fully resolved, with tasks passing at least 95% of tests ("almost resolved") as a secondary reference. Few tasks are fully resolved today, so to measure how team design changes performance we use the finer-grained share of tests passed.
  • Efficiency is the reward gained over the solo PIV agent per $100 of added cost. With asynchronous leads, planning gained 3.4 points per $100, against 1.7 for the next-best stage (implementation). With blocking leads, the gap was smaller (3.8 against 2.4, or 1.6 times).
  • Questions were rare, 6% of worker-to-lead messages. A little under half asked how a worker's piece should connect to the rest, such as which function names or argument types another module expected. Slightly more than a third asked where the reference program had gone after a worker's build overwrote it, and most of the rest asked for the reference program's exact behavior. Sol leads answered 74% of these questions.
  • We also tried Claude Opus 5 on the 30-task subset, but stopped after eight trial tasks all hit an eight-hour timeout. Those tasks cost roughly $500 each, about 15 times what an Opus 4.8 team spent per task.
  • Opus 4.7 was the only model whose solo agent did clearly worse with the PIV prompt than with the minimal one (46.8% against 50.9%). Measured against the solo agent with the same prompt, its PIV teams would have gained 5.5 to 6.4 points. Against its best solo agent, which Figure 10 uses, they gained 1.4 to 2.3.

  • Enterprise AIAgent sprawl: How to manage agent proliferation in the enterpriseOct 15, 20265 min read
  • Enterprise AIAI ROI: How enterprises can measure the return on AI investmentsOct 15, 20266 min read

item.title: [Hugging Face] HiRO-ACEv2: Simulating extreme weather at 3 km resolution fo…
item.description: Full title: HiRO-ACEv2: Simulating extreme weather at 3 km resolution for a fraction of the cost
item.content:encoded:
Back to Articles

HiRO-ACEv2: Simulating extreme weather at 3 km resolution for a fraction of the cost

Enterprise Article

Published October 14, 2026

11

Kyle Wiggers

Ai2Comms

allenai

🤗 Models | 📄 Paper | 📓 Tutorial notebooks | 🌎 Demo

We introduce HiRO-ACEv2, the newest update to our High Resolution Output Ai2 Climate Emulator (HiRO-ACE) system. HiROv2 can reproduce even extremely rare rain, wind, and pressure events with high accuracy, while the full system can generate global 3 km climate data at about 1/300th the cost of X-SHiELD, a high-resolution global atmospheric model that explicitly simulates storms and other small-scale weather.

HiRO-ACE, introduced earlier in 2026, has two parts: ACE, an AI model that operates at a coarser 100 km resolution, and HiRO, a model that sharpens those coarse outputs into fine 3 km detail. The biggest change in HiRO-ACEv2 is the new downscaling model, HiROv2, which can now 1) predict several high-resolution fields at once instead of just rainfall, so it can capture a much wider range of extreme weather, and 2) has improved skill in predicting extreme events.

Our main focus with HiRO-ACEv2 was to simulate extreme events well. Changes to how we train HiROv2 improved its ability to reproduce the most intense rain, wind, and pressure values. When given coarsened X-SHiELD data, it matches the target simulation's high-resolution statistics to within 3%, even for events so rare they occur only once in a million data points. It also accurately estimates the total energy of tropical cyclones, including storms it never saw during training, and generates hurricanes with realistic eyes and rain bands, though winds and pressure around the eye remain somewhat more lopsided than in X-SHiELD. Additionally, HiROv2 realistically generates strong winds flowing down mountain slopes.

We also trained an updated version of ACE for this system. Over a 10-year simulation, its hurricanes, average climate patterns, and overall distributions of rain, wind, and pressure all line up well with X-SHiELD. That tells us ACE's coarse simulations are a solid foundation for producing long-term high-resolution climate data.

Putting HiROv2 and ACE together, we generated a full year of global 3 km data. Its statistics closely match X-SHiELD's, even though HiRO was working from a simulation ACE ran on its own rather than from real X-SHiELD data. Across a 10-year run, the energy of HiRO-ACEv2's hurricanes is comparable to X-SHiELD's over the same period, and snapshots from that run show a variety of other extreme events that resemble those in X-SHiELD.

An example of a strong hurricane in the North Atlantic, generated during the 10-year HiRO-ACEv2 simulation.

Overall, HiRO-ACEv2 offers researchers a flexible and inexpensive way to generate many versions of high-resolution rain, wind, and pressure data for extreme events over 10 years or more. Producing global high-resolution data with it costs roughly 300 times less than running X-SHiELD. If only one region is needed, the savings can be more than a hundred times greater, depending on the size of the area. We're also working on a streamlined version of HiROv2 that could make it more than ten times faster still.

We still have future work ahead of us: because HiRO learned from X-SHiELD, it only works with the version of ACE tuned to match X-SHiELD. That means it can't yet produce high-resolution data for other climates, such as a warmer future or the historical record in datasets like ERA5. Next, we plan to train on new X-SHiELD datasets, including one simulating a world 4°C warmer, so the system can handle different climates. We also plan to add outputs like near-surface temperature and snow and ice, which would allow for even more uses, such as snowpack prediction.

Visualizing and using HiRO outputs

Simulated 10 m wind speed over Baja California in the ACE data visualizer: ACE2 at 100 km resolution on the main map and HiRO-ACEv2 at 3 km in the inset.

A simulated storm over the northeastern Pacific in the ACE data visualizer. The main map shows 10 m wind speed at 100 km resolution; the 3 km HiRO-ACEv2 inset shows finer structure within the storm.

To make it easy to see what HiRO produces without running any inference, we built a web demo that shows pre-generated precipitation, wind, and sea-level pressure output from HiROv1 and HiROv2 side by side with X-SHiELD, the simulation they were trained on. The demo complements the quantitative comparisons in our tech report: it offers a quick visual check of how the outputs look, and lets users zoom in on their own region of interest to judge performance there.

For more in-depth analysis, the models are available to download, and our tutorial notebooks walk through how to run them.

item.title: [OpenRouter] Private Endpoints: Bring Your Fine-Tuned Models and Capacity…
item.description: Full title: Private Endpoints: Bring Your Fine-Tuned Models and Capacity to OpenRouter
item.content:encoded:
Private Endpoints: Bring Your Fine-Tuned Models and Capacity to OpenRouter

Brian Thomas ·10/14/2026

Today we’re launching Private Endpoints. OpenRouter already puts the public models your team uses behind one API. Now it can serve the deployments only your team has too. If you run a fine-tuned model, a dedicated deployment of a public model, or capacity you’ve reserved with a provider, you can route it through OpenRouter alongside everything else in the catalog. Your team keeps the API, model slug, and routing preferences they use today. Private endpoints are only visible within your organization.

Private Endpoints is an add-on to the Enterprise plan. Ask your account representative to enable it for your organization, or talk to the team.

What you can do with it

Fine-tuned models and reserved capacity used to mean a second integration next to OpenRouter. Now you register the deployment as a private endpoint and call it through the API you already use, with public providers as an optional backup if it goes down or hits its rate limit. Only the organizations you approve can see it, and it never shows up in public model lists, rankings, search, charts or benchmarks.

If your organization has a dedicated Azure deployment of DeepSeek V4 Pro for example, you can register it as a private endpoint for deepseek/deepseek-v4-pro and your apps keep calling that slug. For your organization it moves to the front of the provider list by default, and Model Fallbacks, Provider Selection and the rest of routing work as they do for any provider. OpenRouter reaches it with your Azure key through BYOK, so Azure bills you directly.

Reserved capacity gets this treatment too. Point a private endpoint at it and your organization’s traffic goes there first by default. When it’s rate-limited or unavailable, OpenRouter can send the overflow to public providers, within the provider preferences and BYOK fallback settings you’ve set.

Setting up an endpoint

Once Private Endpoints is enabled, an organization admin registers the deployment from the Private Endpoints page in your account. The deployment has to be hosted by a provider we support for BYOK, since OpenRouter reaches it with your own key. It also has to serve a model that’s already in the OpenRouter catalog, since it inherits that model’s slug and capabilities. You can attach your own pricing so the endpoint shows up accurately in cost reporting, and you declare whether the deployment retains prompts.

Before anything routes to the new endpoint, OpenRouter sends one real request through the provider key saved in one of your workspaces. That request proves the key is accepted, the deployment speaks the OpenAI-compatible format, streaming works, usage comes back for billing, and the model ID matches what you registered. Once it passes, you activate the endpoint and workspaces in your organization can call it by the model slug. Until then it stays hidden and can’t be called.

Managing endpoints from code

If you run more than a handful of endpoints, or you keep your infrastructure in code, you can skip the settings page. The Private Endpoints API covers the whole lifecycle, from registering a draft and running the test checks through activation, pricing updates, pausing, and deletion. It’s authenticated with an organization Management API key, and one create call registers, tests, and activates an endpoint.

curl https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/private-endpoints \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $OPENROUTER_MANAGEMENT_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Idempotency-Key: gpt-4o-prod" \
  -d '{
    "model_permaslug": "openai/gpt-4o-2024-08-06",
    "provider_slug": "openai",
    "base_url": "https://api.openai.com/v1",
    "upstream_model_id": "gpt-4o-2024-08-06",
    "pricing": { "prompt": "0.0000025", "completion": "0.00001" },
    "activate": { "workspace_id": "<workspace-id>" }
  }'

If the test checks fail, the draft is kept and comes back with the failed checks, so you can patch it and try again. The Idempotency-Key header makes retries safe (a repeated key returns the endpoint the first request created). The OpenRouter Terraform provider wraps all of this in an openrouter_private_endpoint resource, so terraform apply registers, tests, and activates the endpoint and terraform destroy removes it.

Good to know

  • Marking an endpoint private doesn’t make it a Zero Data Retention endpoint. Your provider handles prompts exactly as it did before, and OpenRouter records the data policy you declare when you register the deployment.
  • A private endpoint can use In-Region Routing if OpenRouter can work out a region from its address, or if you declare one during setup. Requests to us.openrouter.ai or eu.openrouter.ai then route to your deployment inside that region. The In-Region Routing guide lists the supported providers.
  • Your provider key has to be saved under BYOK in each workspace that calls the endpoint, and the test request during setup needs it there too.
  • Each organization can have up to 10 private endpoints by default, and endpoints that are still being set up count toward that limit.

Get started

Private Endpoints is an add-on to the Enterprise plan. Ask your account representative to enable it for your organization, or talk to the team.

Once it’s enabled, an organization admin can add your first endpoint from the Private Endpoints page in your account or with a Management API key through the Private Endpoints API.

Read the docs for more info.

item.title: [Amazon Bedrock] Build self-improving document processing using Amazon Bedroc…
item.description: Full title: Build self-improving document processing using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
item.content:encoded:
Artificial Intelligence

Build self-improving document processing using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore

IDC research shows that document-related challenges cost organizations $19,732 for each information worker annually and reduce productivity by 21.3 percent. Organizations receiving invoices from hundreds of suppliers often face layouts that vary by issuer and change without notice. Template-based systems require constant maintenance at this scale. Staff can spend up to 30 percent of their time on document-related tasks, and manual data entry error rates range from 1–4 percent. Conventional intelligent document processing (IDP) solutions address some of this burden, but they require extensive upfront configuration for each document format and break when layouts vary across vendors.

In this post, you learn how to build an agentic IDP system using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore that classifies, extracts, validates, and learns from business documents with minimal human intervention. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. Your agents automatically handle new document formats, such as supplier invoices, purchase orders, insurance claims, and loan applications. By the end of this post, you can:

  • Deploy a multi-agent IDP system, often in under 20 minutes.
  • Process new document types without manual template configuration.
  • Let agents train themselves on each new document format and reuse what they learn, so later documents of that type go straight to extraction without retraining.

Challenges with rule-based document processing

Many IDP pipelines require you to define templates, extraction rules, and validation logic for every document format upfront. When a new vendor sends a purchase order with a different layout, the pipeline breaks. This creates three core challenges:

  • Template rigidity: Each new document format requires manual configuration, and even minor layout changes can cause extraction failures.
  • No learning: The same extraction errors repeat across similar documents because the system doesn’t retain knowledge from previous corrections.
  • Scaling burden: Each new vendor or document variant multiplies the maintenance effort, and organizations processing documents from hundreds of sources face ongoing operational costs.

An agentic approach addresses these challenges. Instead of static templates, AI agents analyze each document, generate extraction instructions, validate results, and learn from corrections automatically. Over time, your system builds a knowledge base of document formats, so you process similar documents with minimal additional configuration.

Solution overview

In this solution, eight specialized agents collaborate across two graph-based workflows running on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore.

The following diagram shows the multi-agent workflow graph built using Strands Agents, an open source SDK for building AI agents.

Figure 1: Multi-agent orchestration workflow graph

  • Identification workflow: The Analyzer agent extracts text using Amazon Textract and identifies the document type and sender. The Matcher agent searches for similar documents using vector similarity in Amazon S3 Vectors, a capability of Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3).
  • Training workflow (new document types): When no match is found, the Instructions agent generates extraction prompts, the Extractor agent extracts structured data, and the Validator agent checks results against schemas and business rules in Amazon Aurora DSQL. If validation fails, the Instructions Fixer agent refines the prompts and retries. On success, the Save Instructions agent persists the instructions for reuse.
  • Automation workflow (known document types): When a match is found, the Extractor agent uses existing instructions. If validation fails, the Troubleshooter agent fixes the extracted data directly without modifying instructions.

How it works

The following diagram shows the infrastructure architecture for the solution.

Figure 2: Agentic IDP infrastructure architecture on AWS

  • Business documents arrive in Amazon Simple Email Service (Amazon SES) or direct upload to Amazon S3.
  • Amazon EventBridge triggers an AWS Lambda function that creates a tracking job in Amazon DynamoDB and invokes AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore.
  • AgentCore runtime orchestrates document processing through Strands Agents.
  • Your agents securely access AWS resources through machine-to-machine credentials managed by AgentCore Identity, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, and Amazon Cognito.
  • Your Lambda functions become agent-compatible tools through the Model Context Protocol (MCP) interface of AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore.
  • Agents extract text using Amazon Textract, classify documents using vector embeddings in S3 Vectors, and validate data against business rules in Aurora DSQL.
  • Agents access enterprise data through MCP servers to validate extracted content against business rules.
  • You monitor status and troubleshoot issues through a chat-enabled dashboard hosted on Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS).
  • You gain visibility into agent performance through AgentCore Observability, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, and Amazon CloudWatch telemetry.

Deploy the solution

Follow these steps to deploy the solution infrastructure and web UI to your AWS account.

Prerequisites

To deploy this solution, you must have:

  • An AWS account.
  • Access to Amazon Bedrock with Amazon Nova and Anthropic (Claude) models enabled. For model availability by AWS Region, refer to Supported models by AWS Region in Amazon Bedrock.
  • Access to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore (Runtime, Gateway, Identity), S3 Vectors, and Amazon Aurora DSQL in a supported Region.
  • AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK) v2 installed.
  • Docker installed and running (required for building and deploying container images).
  • Python 3.11+ and Node.js 18+.
  • AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) permissions to create S3 buckets, Lambda functions, DynamoDB tables, Cognito user pools, Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) repositories, and Amazon ECS services.
  • Clone the repository and set up the environment: git clone https://github.com/aws-samples/agenticidp-guidance.git cd agenticidp-guidance uv venv source .venv/bin/activate uv pip install -r requirements.txt cd ui/orchestrator npm install cd ../..
  • Deploy the stacks: uv run deploy.py --admin-email your-email@example.com

This deploys six AWS CloudFormation stacks: Core (S3, Cognito, DynamoDB), Gateway (Lambda tools, AgentCore Gateway), Aurora (Amazon Aurora DSQL), Agent (AgentCore runtime, containers), UI Orchestrator (API endpoints), and Modern UI (React app on Amazon CloudFront). Deployment takes approximately 15–20 minutes.

  • Verify deployment by checking that each stack shows CREATE_COMPLETE in the CloudFormation console.

Process files and review results

After deployment, you receive an email with the CloudFront URL, username, and temporary password.

Process a document

  • Sign in to the web UI and choose Process Document.
  • Upload a sample purchase order from infrastructure/sample_data/purchase_orders/training/.
  • The document enters the agent workflow: The Analyzer agent extracts text and identifies the sender and document type. The Matcher agent searches for similar documents in the vector store. For a new document type, the training workflow generates extraction instructions, extracts data, validates it, and saves the instructions for future use. For a known document type, the automation workflow extracts data using existing instructions and validates it.
  • Review results in the Review Jobs and Instructions tab to verify extracted data, validation results, and generated instructions.

Example: A new document type (training workflow)

Suppose you upload the first purchase order from a new retailer, Two Wheel Store. The Matcher agent searches the vector store, finds no similar document, and routes the job through the training workflow.

The Analyzer agent uses Amazon Textract to extract the raw document text:

# PURCHASE ORDER
FROM: Two Wheel Store
Order #: PO-2026-0102-2584
Date: 2026-01-02

## Items Ordered
AC-021  Advanced Computer     Qty: 1   $75.61
        Colors: cr4321        @ $75.61
...
SB-004  Folding Classic       Qty: 8   $9634.32
        Colors: cb8901 I Sizes: S     @ $1204.29

TOTAL: $14931.54

The Instructions agent generates extraction prompts from the schema, and the Extractor agent produces structured JSON:

{
  "po_number": "PO-2026-0102-2584",
  "retailer_name": "Two Wheel Store",
  "order_date": "2026-01-02T00:00:00Z",
  "line_items": [
    { "sku": "AC-021", "product_name": "Advanced Computer", "quantity": 1, "unit_price": 75.61, "line_total": 75.61 },
    { "sku": "SB-004", "product_name": "Folding Classic",   "quantity": 8, "unit_price": 1204.29, "line_total": 9634.32 }
  ],
  "order_total": 14931.54
}

The Validator agent checks the result against the schema and fails:

validation_status: INVALID
error: 'SB-004' does not match '^AB-[A-Z]{2}-\d{3}$'

The vendor’s SKU format (SB-004) doesn’t match Acme Bikes’ internal format (AB-SB-004). The Instructions Fixer agent diagnoses the mismatch and adds an explicit SKU transformation rule to the extraction prompt: prefix vendor SKUs with AB-. On the second pass, the seven line items validate successfully, and the Save Instructions agent persists the refined prompt to the vector store. End-to-end time for this first run: 3 minutes 49 seconds.

Example: A known document type (automation workflow)

When a second purchase order from Two Wheel Store arrives, the Matcher agent finds the stored instructions from the first run with a confidence score of 3.946 (threshold: 3.7) and routes the job through the automation workflow:

  • The Extractor agent applies the stored instructions directly, so the orchestrator skips prompt generation. The SKU transformation rule learned during training applies automatically (EL-002 → AB-EL-002, HB-071 → AB-HB-071, PD-002 → AB-PD-002).
  • The three line items validate on the first pass with an order total of $5,979.19.
  • End-to-end processing completes in 1 minute 30 seconds, down from 3 minutes 49 seconds on the first run.

Use the interactive chat

The dashboard includes a chat interface for troubleshooting:

  • Ask what tools do you have to see available agent capabilities.
  • Ask list instructions to view stored extraction instructions.
  • Ask what is the status of job XXXX to check processing progress.
  • Ask what went wrong with job XXXX, how can we update the instructions? to diagnose failures.

Understand how accuracy improves over time

The system improves over time through two feedback loops:

  • Training loop: When the Instructions Fixer agent refines extraction prompts after validation failures, the improved instructions are saved and reused for similar documents.
  • Processing loop: When the Troubleshooter agent fixes extraction errors, it provides detailed analysis that helps identify patterns in document format variations.

When changing models, use AgentCore Evaluations, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, to confirm that extraction quality remains acceptable. The solution already uses AgentCore Observability, so it has the required instrumentation.

Estimated cost

You pay only for what you use, because the solution runs on serverless and on-demand resources with no idle costs. For a workload of 10 training documents and 1,000 processed documents each month in US East (N. Virginia), the estimated cost is approximately $58 per month. Foundation model (FM) inference through Amazon Bedrock represents approximately 85 percent of the total cost, at roughly $0.055 per document. Actual cost depends largely on the models assigned to each agent. Model choices are centralized in agents/orchestratorgraph/utils/config.py, so you can use lower-cost models for simpler tasks and stronger models where needed. For detailed pricing, refer to the Amazon Bedrock pricing page.

Customize the solution for your use case

You get a purchase order processing use case with a synthetic bike company dataset, a pre-built JSON schema, and a validation Lambda function that checks extracted data against product and vendor records in a mock ERP database. To process your own documents, you must replace the included schemas and validation logic with your own.

Define your document schema

Create a JSON schema that defines the fields you want to extract for each document type. The sample purchase order schema in agents/orchestratorgraph/doc_schema/purchase_order_schema.json provides a reference. Your schema should specify field names, data types, and whether each field is explicitly stated in the document or inferred from context.

Build your validation process

The included validator checks purchase order data against synthetic vendor and product tables in Aurora DSQL. Your production implementation requires a validation process tailored to your business rules. For example:

  • An invoice validator might check vendor IDs against your accounts payable system and verify line item totals match the invoice total.
  • A contract validator might verify that the document contains required clauses and that dates and party names match your records.
  • A claims validator might check policy numbers, coverage limits, and claimant information against your policy management system.

To add a new validator, create a Lambda function that accepts extracted JSON and returns a pass/fail result with detailed error messages, then register it as a tool in AgentCore Gateway. Refer to gateway/tools/po_validator_tool/ for the implementation pattern.

Update agent prompts

The agent prompts in agents/orchestratorgraph/prompts/ reference purchase order terminology. Update these prompts to reflect your document types and extraction requirements. The Orchestrator agent, Validator agent, and Instructions agent each contain document-type-specific language that you should adapt.

Best practices

Keep these recommendations in mind as you train and operate your agentic IDP system.

  • Start with representative samples: Upload 5–10 documents per type during training, including edge cases with format variations, to build reliable extraction instructions.
  • Use business rule validation: Connect validators to your reference data (vendor lists, product catalogs) in Aurora DSQL to catch extraction errors early.
  • Monitor agent performance: Use AgentCore Observability and CloudWatch to track execution paths, identify bottlenecks, and measure extraction accuracy over time.
  • Add document types incrementally: Create a JSON schema for each new document type and a corresponding validation Lambda function. The agents handle the rest.
  • Add guardrails for production: Apply Amazon Bedrock Guardrails to enforce content filtering and grounding checks on agent outputs. This is especially important when you process sensitive document types such as insurance claims or loan applications.
  • Review the OWASP Top 10 for LLMs: Consult the OWASP Top 10 for LLMs and Generative AI Apps for security considerations when building applications that use large language models (LLMs).

Clean up

Important: Before running cleanup, export the data you want to retain. The destroy.py script permanently deletes processed documents (S3), job history (DynamoDB), validation data (Aurora DSQL), and learned extraction instructions (vector store).

To avoid ongoing charges, remove the deployed resources:

uv run destroy.py

Verify that the six CloudFormation stacks are deleted on the console: AgenticIDP-Core-Dev, AgenticIDP-Gateway-Dev, AgenticIDP-Aurora-Dev, AgenticIDP-Agent-Dev, AgenticIDP-UIOrchestr-Dev, and AgenticIDP-ModernUI-Dev.

Conclusion

In this post, you learned how to build a self-improving document processing system using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, where specialized AI agents collaborate to classify, extract, validate, and learn from business documents. This agentic approach adapts to new document formats automatically and improves accuracy over time through feedback loops, replacing manual template configuration with autonomous learning.

As next steps:

  • Deploy the sample solution and test with the included purchase order samples.
  • Add your own document types by creating JSON schemas and validation rules.
